docs.title: Tips for Technical Interviewers
docs.text:
1. Do the problems ahead of time!
  2. Give your candidate an example of an input and the correct solution.
  3. Answer clarifying questions. If the problem doesn’t say, feel free to decide what you want and go with it!
  4. Nervous or overeager candidates tend to jump right into coding or trying to write something down. If this happens, ask your candidate to talk through their ideas first.
  5. If your candidate is quiet, ask them to talk through their ideas aloud. If there’s a silence of more than a couple of minutes, get your candidate talking again.
  6. That said, give your candidate time to think. This is one of the hardest parts of being an interviewer – there are often a lot of pauses and it can be awkward or painful. Two minutes of quiet can feel like a very long time.
  7. If you’re not sure if the candidate is stuck or just thinking and quiet, ask your candidate to explain what they’re thinking. This will help you avoid giving premature or unnecessary hints.
  8. If the candidate is making progress, stay quiet. Sometimes it’s also hard to keep your mouth shut, and it can feel weird to sit there and observe in silence, but when the candidate is excelling, the interviewer does very little talking!
  9. Take notes! Note things that go well and poorly so you can write your full feedback afterwards without interrupting the flow or atmosphere of the interview. Also write down how long the candidate spends on each part (developing the initial algorithm, translating it into code, testing, etcetera) to understand where they struggle and excel.
  10. Encourage the candidate to work through examples by hand and/or draw an illustration of the problem if they’re confused or stuck.
  11. Brainstorm “little hints”, “medium hints”, and “big hints” you can give if the candidate gets stuck. “Little hints” tend to be open-ended (i.e., “how would you do this problem if you were solving it by hand?”) while “big hints” point the candidate to the correct algorithm (i.e., “what would happen if you used data structure X instead of data structure Y?) While “medium hints” unsurprisingly are somewhere in the middle (for example, they might indicate the area in which you want to make a change without giving away the specific change, such as “is there another data structure you could use instead?”).
  12. If they’re stuck, help them talk about their thoughts so far before giving a hint. Often talking through the problem will get an candidate unstuck without any hints by acting as a “rubber duck.” Questions like “and then what?” or “what about when…?” without bringing in any new information are often sufficient to keep the ideas and words flowing.
  13. If you do have to give hints, give them one at a time, in increasing order of difficulty (i.e., start with a “small hint” and only work up to a “big hint” if the candidate is still stuck and running out of time). Leave plenty of space between the hints to give the candidate time to work with them.
  14. Keep track of the time! When time is almost up, tell your candidate you’re almost out of time, and ask them to wrap up their solution as best as possible, such as by explaining what they would do if they had more time. It helps you get a sense of how their thinking has progressed and creates a better experience for them.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A palindrome is a word, phrase, or sequence that reads the same backward as forward. An example of some palindromes are “kayak,” “racecar,” and "rats live on no evil star.” Write a function that takes a string as an input and returns a boolean indicating if the string is a palindrome (the same forwards and backwards) ignoring capitalization, spaces and characters that are not letters.

docs.title: Function Definition
docs.text:
is_palindrome(str) -> bool
str: string
bool: boolean

docs.title: Example Input/Output
docs.text:
Input 1: "noon"
Output 1: True
Input 2: ""
Output 2: True
Input 3: "kayak"
Output 3: True
Input 4: "no"
Output 4: False
Input 5: "step on no pets"
Output 5: True
Input 6: "Was it a car or a cat I saw?"
Output 6: True

docs.title: Possible Solutions
docs.text:
1. Simultaneously iterate over the string forwards and backwards comparing each character. If two characters do not match, return false. If the middle is reached, return true. [Complexity: Optimal; Time: O(n); Space: O(1)]
  2. Recursive. Compare the first and last characters, returning false if they do not match. Recurse on the remainder of the string until a base case (string of length zero or one) is reached. If the base case is reached, return true. [Complexity: Brute Force; Time: O(n); Space: O(n)]
  3. Reverse the string, then compare the reversed and original the same. Return true if they are the same, false otherwise. [Complexity: Brute Force; Time: O(n); Space: O(n)]

If the candidate codes any of these solutions, move on to follow-up 1.

Note: In both the original problem and both follow-ups, boolean flags in the solution can be substituted with an integer count. Additionally, completely correct solutions will ignore characters that are not letters and lowercase (or uppercase) all letters. This is left out of the problem statement to ensure candidates ask identify edge cases and ask appropriate clarifying questions instead of making assumptions. If original solutions do not account for this, remind candidates of this requirement and see if they can update their solution. If they do not make progress in five minutes, this is the one instance in which it is okay to move on without the candidate completing the problem.

docs.title: Follow-Up 1
docs.text: An anagram is a word or phrase formed by rearranging the letters of another. An example of some anagrams are “act” and “cat”; “auctioned” and “cautioned”; and “a gentleman” and “elegant man.” Write a function that takes two strings as input and returns a boolean indicating if the strings are anagrams (the same letters in different orders).

docs.title: Function Definition
docs.text:
are_anagrams(str1, str2) -> bool
str1, str2: string
bool: boolean

docs.title: Example Input/Output
docs.text:
Input 1: "noon", "no"
Output 1: False
Input 2: "on", "no"
Output 2: True
Input 3: "state", "taste"
Output 3: True
Input 4: "teen", "ten"
Output 4: False
Input 5: "the eyes", "they see"
Output 5: True
Input 6: "William Shakespeare", "I'll make a wise phrase"
Output 6: True

docs.title: Possible Solutions
docs.text:
1. Make a map of character to integer. Iterate through string 1, incrementing the count for each character. Iterate through string 2, decrementing the count for each character. Iterate over the map; return false if any value is not 0. Return true if the end is reached. [Complexity: Optimal; Time: O(n); Space: O(n)]
  2. Sort both strings, then compare the sorted strings. Return true if they are the same, false otherwise. [Complexity: Good; Time: O(nlogn); Space: O(n)]
  3. Generate every possible permutation of string 1 and compare each to string 2. Return true if they are the same. If all permutations are checked, return false. [Complexity: Terrible; Time: O(n!), Space: O(n!)]

If the candidate codes solution (1) or (2) move on to follow-up 2. If the candidate proposes solution (3), guide them towards brainstorming other solutions rather than coding it. Do not move on until a viable solution has been coded.

docs.title: Follow-Up 2
docs.text: Now combining the ideas from the previous two parts, the final goal is to determine if a string can be rearranged to form a palindrome. Write a function that takes a string as input and returns a boolean indicating if it is an anagram of a palindrome. Note: if the candidate needs a hint, suggest that rather than trying to use the functions in the previous part, think about what makes a string a palindrome and what makes two strings anagrams.

docs.title: Function Definition
docs.text:
is_palindrome_anagram(str) -> bool
str: string
bool: boolean

docs.title: Example Input/Output
docs.text:
Input 1: "noon"
Output 1: True
Input 2: ""
Output 2: True
Input 3: "dada"
Output 3: True
Input 4: "no"
Output 4: False

docs.title: Possible Solutions
docs.text:
1. Create a map of counts. Iterate over the string, incrementing the count of each character. Initialize a boolean to false to keep track of whether an odd character has been seen. Iterate over the map. If the count is odd and the boolean is already true, return false. If the count is odd and the boolean is still false, update to true. Return true after completing the loop. [Complexity: Optimal; Time: O(n); Space: O(n)]
  2. Create a set of characters. Iterate over the string. For each character, if the character is in the set, remove it, and if it is not in the set, add it. Return true if the set is of size 0 or 1, false otherwise. [Complexity: Optimal; Time: O(n); Space: O(n)]
  3. Initialize a count array of characters (index is integer of character). Iterate over the string and increment the count of every character. Initialize a boolean to false to keep track of whether an odd character has been seen. Iterate over the array. If the count is odd and the boolean is already true, return false. If the count is odd and he boolean is still false, update to true. Return true after completing the loop. [Complexity: Optimal; Time: O(n); Space: O(n)]
  4. Sort the string. Initialize a boolean to false to keep track of whether an odd character has been seen. Iterate over the sorted string, counting occurrences of each character. If the count is odd and the boolean is already true, return false. If the count is odd and the boolean is still false, update to true. Return true after completing the loop. [Complexity: Good, Time: O(nlogn); Space: O(n)]
  5. Use two nested loops to iterate over the string. Initialize a boolean to false to keep track of whether an odd character has been seen. For each character, count the number of times the character appears. If odd and the boolean is already true, return false. If the count is odd and the boolean is still false, update to true. Return true after completing both nested loops. [Complexity: Brute Force; Time: O(n^2); Space: O(1)]
  6. Generate every possible permutation of the string and check whether it is a palindrome. Return true if one is. If all permutations are checked, return false. [Complexity: Terrible; Time: O(n!), Space: O(n!)]

If the candidate codes solution (1), (2), (3), or (4), move on to another question, time permitting. If the candidate codes solution (4), see if you can guide them towards (1), (2), or (3) before moving on. However, if they do not make progress after ~5 minutes, move on. If the candidate proposes solution (5), guide them towards brainstorming other solutions rather than coding it. Do not move on until a viable solution has been coded.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Determine if an array has a majority element (element that appears > n/2 times, where n is the length of the array).

docs.title: Function Definition
docs.text:
has_majority_element(arr) -> int
arr: array of integers
int: integer element in arr

docs.title: Example Input/Output
docs.text:
Input 1: [2, 4, 2, 5, 2, 2, 4]
Output 1: 2
Input 2: [2, 2, 5, 2, 2, 4]
Output 2: 2
Input 3: [4, 2, 5, 2, 2, 4, 3]
Output 3: NULL
Input 4: [2, 4, 5, 3, 2, 4]
Output 4: NULL

docs.title: Possible Solutions
docs.text:
1. Create a map of characters to counts. Increment the counts iterating through the array. Check if any of the counts exceed n/2; if so, a majority element has been found. This solution may be improved by returning early if incrementing a count causes it to cross the n/2 threshold. It can even be further optimized by returning NULL early if there are not sufficient elements remaining to find a majority element. [Complexity: Optimal; Time: O(n); Space: O(n)]
  2. Sort the array. Iterate through the sorted array, counting each character. If a count is greater than n/2, a majority element has been found. [Complexity: Good; Time: O(nlogn); Space: O(n)]
  3. Iterate over the array. For each character, use a nested loop to iterate over the array, counting the number of occurrences. If the number of occurrences is greater than n/2, a majority element has been found. This solution may be improved somewhat by only checking characters in the first half of the array. [Complexity: Brute Force; Time: O(n^2); Space: O(1)]

If the candidate codes solution (1) or (2), move on to follow-up 1. If the candidate codes solution (3), see if you can guide them towards (1) or (2) before moving on. However, if they do not make progress after ~5 minutes, move on.

docs.title: Follow-Up 1
docs.text: Determine if an array has a plurality element (element that appears more than any other element).

docs.title: Function Definition
docs.text:
has_plurality_element(arr) -> int
arr: array of integers
int: integer element in arr

docs.title: Example Input/Output
docs.text:
Input 1: [2, 4, 2, 5, 2, 3, 4]
Output 1: 2
Input 2: [2, 4, 1, 5, 2, 3, 4]
Output 2: NULL
Input 3: [4, 2, 5, 2, 2, 4]
Output 3: 2
Input 4: [4, 2, 4, 2, 2, 4]
Output 4: NULL

docs.title: Possible Solutions
docs.text:
1. Iterate over the array to create a map of elements to counts. Iterate over the map, keeping track of the maximum and a boolean to indicate whether it is unique. At the end, the unique boolean indicates whether a plurality element has been found. [Complexity: Optimal; Time: O(n); Space: O(n)]
  2. Sort the array and keep track of a maximum count and a unique max boolean. Iterate through the sorted array, counting each character. If the number of occurrences is greater than the current max, update the maximum and set the unique max to true. If the number of occurrences is the same as the current max, set the unique max to false. At the end, the unique max indicates whether a plurality element has been found. [Complexity: Good; Time: O(n*logn); Space: O(n)]
  3. Iterate over the array and keep track of a maximum count and a unique max boolean. For each character, use a nested loop to iterate over the array, counting the number of occurrences. If the number of occurrences is greater than the current max, update the maximum and set the unique max to true. If the number of occurrences is the same as the current max, set the unique max to true. At the end, the unique max indicates whether a plurality element has been found. [Complexity: Brute Force; Time: O(n^2); Space: O(1)]

If the candidate codes solution (1) or (2), move on to follow-up 2. If the candidate codes solution (3), see if you can guide them towards (1) or (2) before moving on. However, if they do not make progress after ~5 minutes, move on.

docs.title: Follow-Up 2
docs.text: Determine if an array has an equilibrium index (index where the sum of all elements to the left equals the sum of all elements to the right).

docs.title: Function Definition
docs.text:
has_equilibrium_index(arr) -> int
arr: array of integers
int: integer index in arr

docs.title: Example Input/Output
docs.text:
Input 1: [1, 4, 2, 5, 2, 3, 2]
Output 1: 3
Input 2: [1, 4, 2, 2, 3, 2]
Output 2: NULL
Input 3: [8, 2, 3, 1, 5, 4]
Output 3: 2
Input 4: [6]
Output 4: 0

docs.title: Possible Solutions
docs.text:
1. Iterate over the array left-to-right creating an array of cumulative left sums (excluding the current index). Also iterate over the array right-to-left creating an array of cumulative right sums (also excluding the current index). Iterate over the indices once more, checking both the left and right sum arrays. Return true if the left and right sums are equal. Return false if the end is reached. [Complexity: Optimal; Time: O(n); Space: O(n)]
  2. Iterate over the indices of the array. For each index, use a nested loop to sum the elements to the left and right of the index. Return the index if they are equal. Return NULL if the end of the nested loops are reached. [Complexity: Brute Force; Time: O(n^2); Space: O(1)]

If the candidate codes solution (1), move on to another question, time permitting. If the candidate codes solution (2), see if you can guide them towards (1) before moving on. However, if they do not make progress after ~5 minutes, move on.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Write a partition function that rearranges an array containing odd and even numbers in-place (without creating a new array or sorting the array) so that all odd numbers come before all the even numbers. If the candidate uses a language that does not support pass-by-reference, have them print the resulting array rather than returning it to keep space at O(1).

docs.title: Function Definition
docs.text:
parition_ints(arr) -> void
arr: array of integers

docs.title: Possible Solutions
docs.text:
1. Iterate forwards and backwards through the array simultaneously. Stop the forwards iteration when an even number is reached and the backwards iteration when an odd number is reached. Swap them. Advance both pointers. Continue until the forwards and backwards indices cross. [Complexity: Optimal; Time: O(n); Space: O(1)]
  2. Iterate through the array. At each index, if it contains an even element, iterate through the rest of the array until an odd element is found and swap them. When no element to swap with is found or the iteration ends the process is complete. [Complexity: Brute Force; Time: O(n^2); Space: O(1)]
  3. Iterate through the array. At each index, if it contains an even element, save that element in a temp value and shift all elements to the right of it one to the left. Insert that element into the end slot in the array [Complexity: Brute Force; Time: O(n^2); Space: O(1)]

If the candidate proposes the solution in which a new array is created and first the even numbers are copied and then the odds, remind them of the in-place requirement and guide them towards one of the other solutions before they code. If the candidate codes solution (1), move on to follow-up 1. If the candidate codes solutions (2) or (3) see if you can guide them towards (1) before moving on. However, if they do not make progress after ~5 minutes, move on.

docs.title: Follow-Up 1
docs.text: Now suppose we want to separately partition zeros. In the partitioned array, zeros should be between the odd and the other even integers. Again, if the candidate uses a language that does not support pass-by-reference, have them print the resulting array rather than returning it to keep space at O(1).

docs.title: Function Definition
docs.text:
partition_ints(arr) -> void
arr: array of integers

docs.title: Possible Solutions
docs.text:
1. Iterate through the array and count the even and odd integers. Iterate forwards and backwards through the array simultaneously. Stop the forwards iteration when an even number or 0 is reached and the backwards iteration when an odd number or 0 is reached. Swap them. Advance the forwards pointer if it is on an odd number or the index is greater than or equal to the number of odd numbers; advance the backwards pointer if it is on an even number or the index is less than the total elements minus the even elements. Continue until the forwards iteration until and backwards indices cross. [Complexity: Optimal; Time: O(n); Space: O(1)]
  2. Use two passes. First partition the array into evens and odds or zeros. Iterate forwards and backwards through the array simultaneously. Stop the forwards iteration when an even number is reached and the backwards iteration when an odd number or a zero is reached. Swap them. Advance both pointers. Continue until the forwards and backwards indices cross. Do a second pass, iterating forwards and backwards on the subarray containing odd numbers and zeros (0 through the final position of the backwards pointer) simultaneously. Stop the forwards iteration when a zero is reached and the backwards iteration when an odd number is reached. Swap them. Advance both pointers. [Complexity: Optimal; Time: O(n); Space: O(1)] Note: of course it is possible to instead first partition the array the other way, into evens or zeros and odds.
  3. The brute force swapping solution (2) from the original problem, swapping even and zero elements for odds. Use a flag to indicate whether odd numbers remain. When no more odd numbers remain, continue, swapping evens for zeros. Continue until no more zeros are found or the iteration completes. [Complexity: Brute Force; Time: O(n^2); Space: O(1)]
  4. The brute force shifting solution (3) from the original problem. Use a flag to indicate whether odd numbers remain. Shift when a zero or an even element is encountered. When no more odd numbers remain, shift when an even element is encountered. [Complexity: Brute Force; Time: O(n^2); Space: O(1)]

If the candidate proposes the solution in which a new array is created and first the negative numbers are copied, then the zeros, then the odds, remind them of the in-place requirement and guide them towards one of the other solutions before they code. If the candidate codes solution (1) or (2), move on to follow-up 2. If the candidate codes solutions (3) or (4) see if you can guide them towards (1) or (2) before moving on. However, if they do not make progress after ~5 minutes, move on.

docs.title: Follow-Up 2
docs.text: Now suppose the array only contains 0s, 1s, and 2s.

docs.title: Function Definition
docs.text:
partition_ints(arr) -> int
arr: array of integers
int: integer index in arr

docs.title: Possible Solutions
docs.text:
1. Count each element and store the results in a map. Initialize a sorted constant array of the three possible elements. Initialize an index counter to zero. Iterate over the constant array, looking up the count of each element in the map and overwriting the appropriate number of indices in the original array with the element from the constant array. [Complexity: Optimal; Time: O(n); Space: O(1)]
  2. Count each element and store the results in variables. Initialize an index counter to zero. In the correct order, go through the variables and overwrite the appropriate number of indices in the original array with the element the variable represents. [Complexity: Optimal; Time: O(n); Space: O(1)] Note: while the complexity of this solution is the same as (1), it is much messier as it uses three variables instead of a data structure and relies on the knowledge of “magic numbers.”
  3. Any of the solutions from follow-up (1) will also work. [Complexity: Varies]

If the candidate proposes the solution in which a new array is created and first the negative numbers are copied, then the zeros, then the odds, remind them of the in-place requirement and guide them towards one of the other solutions before they code. If the candidate proposes (3), this is good insight but ask if it can be improved upon by using the additional constraints in the follow-up if they do not suggest doing so themselves. Do not move on until the candidate codes solution (1) or (2). If the candidate codes solution (2), see if you can guide them towards solution (1) before moving on to another question. However, if they do not make progress after ~5 minutes, move on.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Given an array of integers, create an array where each index has the sum of all the elements in the original array except for the element at that index.

docs.title: Function Definition
docs.text:
other_sum_array(arr) -> sum_arr
arr: array of integers
sum_arr: array of integers

docs.title: Possible Solutions
docs.text:
1. Iterate over the array and sum the elements. Iterate again and for each element subtract that element from the sum. Add the difference to the results array. [Complexity: Optimal; Time: O(n); Space: O(1)]
  2. Iterate over the array forwards and backwards to create partial forward sum and backward sum arrays such that each index contains the sum of all the elements before but not including that index. Iterate over the indices once more. The result for each index is the sum of partial forward sum and partial backward sum for that index. [Complexity: Almost Optimal; Time: O(n); Space: O(n)]
  3. Use a nested loop to iterate over the indices. For each index, iterate over the array, summing all the elements except the one at that index. [Complexity: Brute Force; Time: O(n^2); Space: O(n)]

If the candidate codes solution (1) or (2), move on to follow-up 1. If the candidate codes solution (3), see if you can guide them towards (1) or (2) before moving on. However, if they do not make progress after ~5 minutes, move on.

docs.title: Follow-Up 1
docs.text: Now create an array where each index has the product of all the elements in the original array except for the element at that index.

docs.title: Function Definition
docs.text:
other_product_array(arr) -> prod_arr
arr: array of integers
prod_arr: array of integers

docs.title: Possible Solutions
docs.text:
1. Iterate over the array and multiply the elements. Iterate again and for each element divide the product by that element. The thing that is different, and more challenging, than in the original problem is handling the 0-element case. Keep a set of zero element indices. Do not multiply zero elements. If the final set size is one, set that index to the product and every other index to zero. If the set size is zero, set all indices to zero. Add the difference to the results array. [Complexity: Optimal; Time: O(n); Space: O(n)]
  2. Iterate over the array forwards and backwards to create partial forward product and backward product arrays such that each index contains the product of all the elements before but not including that index. Iterate over the indices once more. The result for each index is the product of partial forward product and partial backward product for that index. [Complexity: Optimal; Time: O(n); Space: O(n)]
  3. Use a nested loop to iterate over the indices. For each index, iterate over the array, multiplying all the elements except the one at that index. [Complexity: Brute Force; Time: O(n^2); Space: O(n)]

If the candidate codes solution (1) or (2), move on to follow-up 1. If the candidate codes solution (3), see if you can guide them towards (1) or (2) before moving on. However, if they do not make progress after ~5 minutes, move on.

docs.title: Follow-Up 2
docs.text: Now given a 2D array (matrix), create a 2D array (matrix) where each index i,j is the sum of all the indices in the rectangle from 0,0 (upper left corner) to i,j (lower right corner). Note: this problem can be hard to understand from just words. Show the example and explain how the output is derived from the input.

docs.title: Function Definition
docs.text:
sum_matrix(mat) -> sum_mat
mat: 2D array of integers
sum_mat: 2D array of integers

docs.title: Possible Solutions
docs.text:
1. Iterate over the first row and the first column. Set (r, 0) in the result array to the sum of (r-1, 0) in the result array and (r, 0) in the original array; set (0, c) in the result array to the sum of (0, c-1) in the result array and (0,c) in the original array. Iterate from (1,1), setting (r, c) in the result array to the sum of (r-1, c) + (r, c-1) - (r-1, c-1) in the result array and (r, c) in the original array. [Complexity: Optimal; Time: O(n)/O(r*c); Space: O(1)]
  2. For each row-column index, iterate over the matrix up to that row and column summing the elements. Set that index in the result array to this sum. [Complexity: Brute Force; Time: O(n^2)/O(r^2*c^2); Space: O(1)]

If the candidate codes either solution, move on to another question, time permitting, unless the candidate proposes improving solution (2) to solution (1).

docs.title: Tips for Interviewers
docs.text:
1. Do the problems ahead of time!
  2. Give your candidate an example of an input and the correct solution.
  3. Answer clarifying questions. If the problem doesn’t say, feel free to decide what you want and go with it!
  4. Nervous or overeager candidates tend to jump right into coding or trying to write something down. If this happens, ask your candidate to talk through their ideas first.
  5. If your candidate is quiet, ask them to talk through their ideas aloud. If there’s a silence of more than a couple of minutes, get your candidate talking again.
  6. That said, give your candidate time to think. This is one of the hardest parts of being an interviewer – there are often a lot of pauses and it can be awkward or painful. Two minutes of quiet can feel like a very long time.
  7. If you’re not sure if the candidate is stuck or just thinking and quiet, ask your candidate to explain what they’re thinking. This will help you avoid giving premature or unnecessary hints.
  8. If the candidate is making progress, stay quiet. Sometimes it’s also hard to keep your mouth shut, and it can feel weird to sit there and observe in silence, but when the candidate is excelling, the interviewer does very little talking!
  9. Take notes! Note things that go well and poorly so you can give feedback afterwards without interrupting the flow or atmosphere of the interview. Also write down how long the candidate spends on each part (developing the initial algorithm, translating it into code, testing, etcetera) to understand where they struggle and excel.
  10. Encourage the candidate to work through examples by hand and/or draw an illustration of the problem if they’re confused or stuck.
  11. Brainstorm “little hints”, “medium hints”, and “big hints” you can give if the candidate gets stuck. “Little hints” tend to be open-ended (i.e., “how would you do this problem if you were solving it by hand?”) while “big hints” point the candidate to the correct algorithm (i.e., “what would happen if you used data structure X instead of data structure Y?) While “medium hints” unsurprisingly are somewhere in the middle (for example, they might indicate the area in which you want to make a change without giving away the specific change, such as “is there another data structure you could use instead?”).
  12. If they’re stuck, help them talk about their thoughts so far before giving a hint. Often talking through the problem will get an candidate unstuck without any hints by acting as a “rubber duck.” Questions like “and then what?” or “what about when…?” without bringing in any new information are often sufficient to keep the ideas and words flowing.
  13. If you do have to give hints, give them one at a time, in increasing order of specificity (i.e., start with a “small hint” and only work up to a “big hint” if the candidate is still stuck and running out of time). Leave plenty of space between the hints to give the candidate time to work with them.
  14. Keep track of the time! When time is almost up, tell your candidate you’re almost out of time, and ask them to wrap up their solution as best as possible, such as by explaining what they would do if they had more time. It helps you get a sense of how their thinking has progressed and creates a better experience for them.
  15. Stay in character until the interview is over! You’re the interviewer, not a peer or teacher. The best mocks are the ones that most closely replicate a true interview.
  16. After the interview ends, break your interviewer character and switch to mentor mode. Leave enough time to give face-to-face constructive feedback. Give honest feedback so candidates can avoid repeating mistakes from mock interviews in real interviews! Not pointing out mistakes is not neutral - it actually encourages candidates to repeat those mistakes. Include feedback on both technical skills and soft skills, and be sure to also point out what the candidate did well so they know to keep doing it.

docs.title: First Element Occurring K Times in an Array
docs.text: Given an array and an integer k, return the first element that occurs k times.

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
For each element in the array, iterate through the array and count the number of occurrences. If it occurs k or more times, return the element, otherwise continue to the next element.

Complexity:

Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(1)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Keep a map of element counts. Iterate through the array, incrementing the count of each element in a map. If the count equals k, return the element.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

C++ Sample Code

#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

int firstKRepeats(vector<int> &vec, int k) {
    auto counts = unordered_map<int, int>();
    for (int x: vec) {
       counts[x]++;
       if (counts[x] == k)
           return x;
    }
    // Agree on a value to return here.
    // If you stipulate the values are positive, -1 works well.
    return -1;
}

docs.title: Follow-Up
docs.text:
What about if we wanted the last element occurring K times?

Instead of returning when we find an element that occurs k times, we can update a variable keeping track of the last time an element occurring k times was seen. Note that iterating backwards does not work, because an element that occurs more than k times may incorrectly be returned. Time and space complexity are the same as in the original problem.

docs.title: Missing Elements in a Range
docs.text: Given an array and two integers, lo and hi, defining a range, return the values in the range missing from the array.

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Sort the array, then perform a binary search for the low value. Traverse from where it is (or is not found) until the high value and store the missing numbers in an array. (Equivalently, search for the high value and traverse backwards to the low value.)

Complexity:

Time: O(nlogn)

Space: O(logn) or O(n) extra space, depending on the sorting algorithm; most built-in sorts are quicksort, which is O(logn). Also O(k) required space for the return value, where k is the size of the range.

docs.title: Almost Optimal
docs.text:
Iterate over the array, creating a set of the array elements. Iterate over the range, checking the set for the value at each iteration and adding it to an array if not present.

Complexity:

Time: O(n + k) or, equivalently, O(max(n, k))

Space: O(n) extra space. Also O(k) required space for the return value, where k is the size of the range.

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Iterate over the array, adding each element in the range to a set. Iterate over the range, checking the set for the value at each iteration and adding it to an array if not present.

Complexity:

Time: O(n + k) or, equivalently, O(max(n, k))

Space: O(min(n, k)) extra space. Also O(k) required space for the return value, where k is the size of the range.

C++ Sample Code

#include <unordered_set>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

vector<int> missingFromRange(vector<int> &vec, int lo, int hi) {
    auto present = unordered_set<int>();
    auto missing = vector<int>();
    for (int x: vec)
       if (x >= lo && x <= hi)
           present.insert(x);
    for (int i = lo; i <= hi; i++)
       if (present.count(i) == 0)
           missing.push_back(i);
    return missing;
}

docs.title: Pangrams
docs.text: A pangram is a phrase or sentence containing every letter (a-z) in the English alphabet. Given a string, determine if it is a pangram.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Input: “The quick brown fox jumps over the dog”

Output: False

Input: “The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog”

Output: True

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Convert the string to lowercase. Iterate over the lowercase alphabet and search the string for the letter. If the letter is not found, return false. If the end of the alphabet is reached, return true.

Complexity:

Time: O(n); O(n*m) where m is the size of the alphabet

Space: O(1)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Create an alphabet array of 0s of size 26. Convert the string to lowercase. Iterate over the string. Convert the current character to an integer and shift (so a-z are 0-25). If the integer representation is 0-25, set the value at that index to 1. Iterate over the alphabet array. If a 0 is encountered, return false. If the end of the array is reached, return true. (Equivalently, a set or map can be used.)

Complexity:

Time: O(n); O(n+m) where m is the size of the alphabet (considering the alphabet size as a constant, the brute force and optimal are the same; if the candidate codes the brute force solution and states this encourage them to think of a solution that scales for a larger alphabet)

Space: O(n)

C++ Sample Code

#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>

using namespace std;

bool is_pangram(string str) {
    lower = transform(str.begin(), str.end(), tolower);
    auto alpha = vector<bool>(26, False);
    for (char c: str) {
       int ascii_shift = c - 'a';
       if (ascii_shift >= 0 && ascii_shift < 26)
            alpha[ascii_shift] = True;
    }
    for (bool b: alpha)
       if (!b) return False
    return True;
}

docs.title: Isomorphic Strings
docs.text: Two strings are considered isomorphic if the characters in one string can be replaced to get the characters in the other string. No two distinct characters can be replaced by the same character, but a character can be replaced with itself.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Input: “egg”, “add”

Output: True

Input: “foo”, “bar”

Output: False

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Return false if the strings are of unequal length. Iterate over the length of the strings. For each index, iterate backwards in each string until the same character is found or the beginning is reached. If the previous occurrence of each character is not the same, return false. If the end of the strings are reached, return true. Note: many variations of the same solution exist.

Complexity:

Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(1)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Return false if the strings are of unequal length. Create two maps representing the mappings from string one to string two and vice versa. Iterate over the length of the strings. If the current characters are not in the maps keyed on the respective strings, add them with the character in the other string as the value. If one is in its map and not the other, return false. If they are both in the map, return false if they do not correspond, and continue if they do. Return true if the end of the strings are reached. Note: many variations of the same solution exist.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

C++ Sample Code

#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <unordered_map>

using namespace std;

bool are_isomorphic(string str1, string str2) {
     if (str1.size() != str2.size()) return False;
     auto map1 = unordered_map<char, char>();
     auto map2 = unordered_map<char,char>();
     for (int i = 0; i < str1.size(); i++) {
         if ((map1.find(str1[i]) == map1.end()) != (map2.find(str2[i]) == map2.end()))
              return False
         if((map1.find(str1[i]) == map1.end()) {
              map1[str1[i]] = str2[i];
              map2[str2[i]] = str1[i];
         } else if (map1[str1[i]] != str2[i] || map2[str2[i]] != str1[i])
              return False;
     }
     return True;
}

docs.title: Subarrays of Size K Containing Duplicates
docs.text: Given an array of integers and an integer k, return the number of unique subarrays of size k that contain duplicate elements.

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Create a count. Iterate through the array. For each index, iterate through the rest of the array until a duplicate is encountered. If the indices are k or fewer apart, increment the count.

Complexity:

Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(1)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Create a map of integers to integers. Add the first k elements to the map, incrementing their counts. Initialize a count of subarrays to zero if there are no duplicates in the first k elements and 1 otherwise. Iterate over the array until i + k is out-of-bounds. For each index i, decrement the count of the element at i in the map and increment the count of the element at i + k. Check the map for values greater than 1; if there are any, increment the count of subarrays.

Complexity:

Time: O(n) or O(n*k)

Space: O(1) or O(k)

C++ Sample Code

#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>

using namespace std;

int dupKSubArrays(vector<int> &vec, int k) {
    auto window = unordered_map<int>();
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) {
        window[vec[i]]++;
        if (window[vec[i]] > 1)
            count = 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < vec.size() - k; i++) {
        window[vec[i]]--;
        window[vec[i+k]]++;
        for (int element : window)
            if (element.second > 1) {
                count++;
                break;
           }
    }
    return count;
}

docs.title: Max Stock Profit with Single Buy/Sell
docs.text: Given an array of integers representing the price of a stock over time, return the maximum profit that can be made on a share by buying and selling at most once.

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Keep track of the max profit (initialized to zero) in a variable. Use a nested loop to check the profit at every possible buy/sell combination and compare to the max profit so far.

Complexity:

Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(1)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Use two variables to keep track of the max profit and the buy point (both initialized to zero). Iterate through the array. If the current value is less than the value at the buy point, update the buy point to the current index. Otherwise, compute the profit with the current index as the sell point and compare to the max profit so far.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

C++ Sample Code

#include <vector>

using namespace std;

int stockProfit(vector<int> &vec) {
    int profit = 0;
    int buy = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < vec.size(); i++)
        if (vec[i] < vec[buy])
             buy = i;
        else if (vec[i] - vec[buy] > profit) {
             profit = vec[i] - vec[buy];
    return profit;
}

docs.title: Follow-Up
docs.text:
What if we were allowed unlimited buys and sells?

Iterate over the array. If the next element is greater than the current element, add the difference to the profit.

docs.title: Number of Triplets with Zero Sum
docs.text: Given an array of integers, return the number of unique triplets that sum to zero.

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Keep a count of triplets. Use a triple nested loop to iterate through every possible triplet of indices and check whether the sum of the elements equals zero and if so, increment the count.

Complexity:

Time: O(n^3)

Space: O(1)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Create a map of integers to integers. Iterate through the array and increment the count of each element. Use a nested loop to iterate through every possible pair of indices. Calculate the target value by negating the sum of the two elements. If the target is in the map and the count of the target is greater than or equal to the occurrences of the target in the triplet, increment the count.

Complexity:

Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(n)

C++ Sample Code

#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>

using namespace std;

int tripletsZeroSum(vector<int> &vec) {
    auto counts = unordered_map<int>();
    int count = 0;
    for (int element : vec)
        counts[element]++;
    for (int i = 0; i < vec.size(); i++)
        for (int j = i+1; j < vec.size(); j++) {
            int target = -1 * (vec[i] + vec[j]);
           if (counts.find(target) == counts.end())
               continue;
           if (vec[i] == target && vec[j] == target && counts[target] < 3)
               continue;
           if (vec[i] == target || vec[j] == target && counts[target] < 2)
               Continue;
           count++;
        }
    return count;
}

docs.title: Follow-Up
docs.text:
What about if we wanted the number of triplets summing to any given target?

Pass the target sum to the function and calculate the value to lookup in the map by subtracting the sum of the pair from that value.

docs.title: Max Meetings in a Room
docs.text: Given an array of numeric pairs representing the start and end times of scheduled meetings, find the maximum number of meetings that can be held in a room if only one meeting can occur in the room at once.

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Check if any of the meetings overlap. If not, return the number of meetings. Otherwise, try removing each of the overlapping meetings and repeat.

Complexity:

Time: O(n!) (Do not even let the candidate code this solution.)

Space: O(1)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Sort the meetings by end time. Initialize a count to one and index (to track the last selected meeting) to 0. Iterate through the meetings starting at index 1. If the last selected meeting’s end time is less than or equal to the current meeting’s start time, the meeting can be held in the same room; increment the count and update the index to the current index.

Complexity:

Time: O(nlogn)

Space: O(1)

C++ Sample Code

#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>

using namespace std;

int maxMeetingsRoom(vector<pair<float, float>> &vec) {
    if (!vec.size())
       return 0;
    sort(vec.begin(), vec.end(), [](const pair<int, int> &left, const pair<int, int> &right) {
        if (left.second != right.second)
            return left.second < right.second;
        else
            return left.first < right.first;
    });
    int count = 1;
    int ind = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i < vec.size(); i++)
        if (vec[i].first >= vec[ind].second) {
            count++;
            ind = i;
        }
    return count;
}

docs.title: Reverse Linked List in Groups of k
docs.text: Given the head node of a linked list, reverse the linked list in groups of k.

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Iterate over the linked list and copy it to a temporary array. Iterate over the array using the indices to reverse the elements in groups of k. (One optimal variation of this is to use nested loops with an outer loop that increments i by k, rather than the typical 1, and an inner loop that iterates only over i to i +k, reversing the elements.) Iterate over the linked list again, overwriting the data with the corresponding element in the array.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

docs.title: Good
docs.text:
Reverse the first k elements recursively using a counter for k. Recurse on the remainder of the list, setting element k’s next to the result.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n/k) (O(1) explicit, O(n/k) implicit recursive stack space)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Reverse the first k elements iteratively using a counter for k. Recurse on the remainder of the list, setting element k’s next to the result.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

C++ Sample Code

using namespace std;

Node *kReverse(Node *head, int k) {
    int count = 0;
    Node *curr = head;
    Node *next = nullptr;
    Node *prev = nullptr;
    Node *newHead = nullptr;
    Node *newTail = nullptr;
    Node *tail = nullptr;
    while (curr) {
        count = k;
        join = curr;
        prev = nullptr;
        while (curr && count--) {
            next = curr->next;
            curr->next = prev;
            prev = curr;
            curr = next;
        }
        if (!newHead)
             newHead = prev;
        if (tail)
             tail->next = prev;
        tail = newTail;
    }
    return newHead;
}

docs.title: Max Height of a Binary Tree
docs.text: Given a binary tree, find the longest path from the root to a leaf (node with no children).

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Use any traversal to find every leaf node. Then use any traversal to find the distance to each leaf node. Return the maximum.

Complexity

Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(n)

Note: do not let the candidate code this solution!

docs.title: Good
docs.text:
Use a post-order traversal to calculate the heights of the left and right subtrees and return the max plus one.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n) (O(1) explicit, O(n) implicit stack space)

docs.title: Good
docs.text:
Use a level-order traversal using either two queues for current and previous level or pushing null values (if permitted in the language of choice) to mark the end of levels. If the former, keep a level count that is incremented every time the current level is reset; if the latter, keep a level count that is incremented whenever a null value is popped.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
The Morris traversal algorithm makes this possible in O(1) space. It is not expected that candidates will find this solution; therefore the sample solution below is a “good” solution.

C++ Sample Code

#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int maxDepth(Node *root) {
    if (!root)
        return 0;
    return 1 + max(maxDepth(root->left), maxDepth(root->right));
}

docs.title: Number of Nodes within K Distance of Root
docs.text: Given a binary tree, count the number of nodes within k distance of the root.

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Use any traversal to find every node. Then use any traversal to find the depth of each node. Count the number of values less than or equal to k.

Complexity

Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(n)

Note: do not let the candidate code this solution!

docs.title: Better
docs.text:
Use a level-order or pre-order traversal to find the depth of each node. Count the number of values less than or equal to k.

Complexity

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

Note: do not let the candidate code this solution!

docs.title: Good
docs.text:
Use a level-order traversal using either two queues for current and previous level. Keep two counts: a level count that is incremented every time the current level is reset; and a node count that is incremented every time a node is popped. When the level count exceeds k, return the node count.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

Note that while Big O space and time are the same as the “Better” solution, because this solution terminates early, in practice it is much better.

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Use a pre-order traversal that accepts the distance from the root and k. Increment the distance; if it is greater than k, return 0; otherwise return one plus the counts from the left and right subtrees.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(k) (O(1) explicit, O(k) implicit stack space)

Note: in the worst case (k=n), the max space for the “Good” solution is n/2 and the max space for the “Optimal” solution is n, since we typically consider k \<\< n, the solutions are labelled this way. However, both are acceptable. If the candidate considers and weighs this, that is the ideal, although not expected.

C++ Sample Code

#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int countWithinK(Node *root, int k, int depth) {
    if (!root || depth+1 > k)
        return 0;
    return 1 + countWithinK(root->left, k, depth+1), countWithinK(root->right, k, depth+1));
}

int countWithinK(Node *root, int k) {
    return countWithinK(root, k, 0);
}

docs.title: Median of a Sorted Linked List
docs.text: Given a sorted singly list of integers, return the median value.

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Copy the linked list into an array and use the indices to find the median.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

Note: do not let the candidate code this solution!

docs.title: Good
docs.text:
Iterate over the list to find its length. Then iterate again to find the middle(s).

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Use fast-slow pointers to find the middle(s) at the same time as the length.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

Note: the Big O is the same as the “Good” solution but a traversal is eliminated, making this the better solution.

C++ Sample Code

using namespace std;

Node *median(Node *head) {
    Node *slow = head;
    Node *fast = head;
    int count = 0;
    while (fast) {
        count++;
        fast = fast->next;
        if (fast) {
            count++;
            fast = fast->next;
            if (fast->next)
                slow = slow->next;
        }
    }
    if (count % 2)
        return slow->next->value;
    return (slow->value + slow->next->value) / 2;
}

docs.title: Count Paths Between Nodes
docs.text: Given a graph, an origin node, and a destination node, count the number of distinct paths from the origin to the destination.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Input graph:

A: B, D, E

B: A, C

C: B, D

D: A, C

E: A

Origin: A, Destination: D

Output: 2 (Possible paths are [A, D] and [A, B, C, D])

Origin: B, Destination: D

Output: 2 (Possible paths are [B, A, D] and [B, C, D])

Note: the problem does not specify undirected. The solution should also work for directed graphs. The candidate should seek this clarification.

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Generate every possible permutation of 0 to n-2 nodes (excluding the origin and destination). Traverse each, checking whether the edges exist. If all do, increase count of paths.

Complexity:

Time: O(n!)

Space: O(2^n)

Note: do not let the candidate code this solution!

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Use DFS to traverse the graph from the origin. Rather than terminating when the destination is found as you would to find whether a path exists, increase the count of paths and continue traversing until all possible paths are exhausted. To increase the count, return 0 if the destination is not found and 1 if it is, adding the result of the recursive call to a running sum.

Complexity:

Time: O(V+E)

Space: O(V)

docs.title: Topping Possibilities
docs.text: A sandwich shop has n available toppings a customer can add to a build-your-own sandwich. Given a list of the available toppings, return every possible combination of toppings a customer could order.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Input: [“cheese”]

Output: [ [ ], [“cheese”] ]

Input: [“cheese”, “onions”, “pesto”]

Output: [ [ ], [“cheese”], [“onions”], [“pesto”], [“cheese”, “onions”], [“cheese”, “pesto”], [“onions”, “pesto”], [“cheese”, “onions”, “pesto”] ]

docs.title: Brute Force/Optimal
docs.text:
In this problem, the brute force and the optimal solution are the same: there is no choice but to generate every possible combination of toppings. Use a queue to store the results. Start with an empty array on the queue. Iterate over the list of toppings and their index, i. Remove 2^i items from the front of the queue. For each removed list, add two lists to the back of the queue: the same list that was removed, and the removed list with the element in the toppings list at index i added to it. Insert the elements in the resulting queue into an array return it.

Complexity:

Time: O(2^n)

Space: O(2^n)

docs.title: Alien Dictionary
docs.text: You are given a list of words in an alien language, sorted alphabetically according to that language. The language uses the letters from the English alphabet but they do not represent the English letters. Determine the order of the letters in the alien alphabet.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Input: “bzza”, “baj”, “zja”, “zb”, “kaab”, “kkz”

Output: ‘j’, ‘b’, ‘z’, ‘a’, ‘k’

Input: “at”, “cocoa”, “cot”, “cat”, “god”, “dot”, “dog”

Output: ‘o’, ‘a’, ‘c’, ‘t’, ‘g’, ‘d’

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Generate every possible alphabetical ordering. Sort according to that ordering and compare to the input.

Complexity:

Time: O(n!) where n is the number of characters, not words

Space: O(n!) where n is the number of characters, not words

Note: do not let the candidate code this solution!

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Treat the problem as a topological sort graph problem. Unique letters represent nodes. Create edges as follows: iterate over the words, looking at pairs of adjacent words, words n and n+11. Iterate over the indices of the characters in words n and n+1 until you find the first index i at which n[i] and n+1[i] are not the same and create an edge form n[i] to n+1[i]. Then perform topological sort.

Note: ensure the candidate clarifies and appropriately accounts the edge case in which there is not enough information to conclusively determine the order.

Complexity:

Time: O(V+E) or O(n^2) where n is the number of characters, not words

Space: O(V) or O(n^2) where n is the number of characters, not words

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Complexity:

Time: O(2^n)

Space: O(2^n)

C++ Sample Code

docs.title: Reorganize Array without Adjacent Duplicates
docs.text: Given an array of integers, reorder the elements so that no two adjacent elements are the same.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Note: there are multiple possible outputs for many inputs. One solution is illustrated below. Any is acceptable; answer this question if it is asked but do not bring it up without the candidate introducing it.

Input: [1, 5, 4, 3, 8, 4]

Output: [1, 5, 4, 3, 8, 4]

Input: [3, 4, 1, 1, 3, 4, 3, 3, 4]

Output: [3, 4, 3, 4, 3, 1, 3, 4, 1]

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Create a map of elements to counts. Try every possible solution and check whether there are any adjacent duplicates. Return the first valid solution. Do not let the candidate code this solution.

Complexity:

Time: O(n!)

Space: O(n!)

docs.title: Bad
docs.text:
Create a map of elements to counts. Use recursion with backtracking and branchtrimming to build the solution array from the elements, terminating a branch if it puts two duplicate elements next to each other.

Complexity:

Time: O(n!) but in practice much better than the brute force

Space: O(n)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Create a map of elements to counts and initalize a previous element to null. Use a priority queue and insert each element with its count as the weight. Remove the top element, insert it into the solution array and decrement the count. Insert the previous element, if there is one and its count is not zero, back into the priority queue and save the updated top element as the previous element. Repeat until priority queue is empty. If the previous element has a zero count, return the solution array; otherwise there is no possible solution.

Complexity:

Time: O(nlogn)

Space: O(n)

C++ Sample Code

docs.title: Peer Mock Interviews
docs.text: Resources for fellows who run mock interviews with each other: tips for peer interviewers and the question bank, with solutions.

docs.title: Directions
docs.text:
• Select one of the questions you were asked in a previous mock interview.
  • If your partner finishes early, choose another question you were asked in a previous mock interview.
  • Do not use a question your partner was already asked in a previous mock interview. We have paired you to ensure you and your partner were asked at least two different questions in the first three mock interviews.

docs.title: Tips for Interviewers
docs.text:
1. Ask questions you have already solved!
  2. Give your partner an example of an input and the correct solution.
  3. Answer clarifying questions. If the problem doesn’t say, feel free to decide what you want and go with it!
  4. Nervous or overeager interviewees tend to jump right into coding or trying to write something down. If this happens, ask your partner to talk through their ideas first.
  5. If your interviewee is quiet, ask them to talk through their ideas aloud. If there’s a silence of more than a couple of minutes, get your interviewee talking again.
  6. That said, give your interviewee time to think. This is one of the hardest parts of being an interviewer – there are often a lot of pauses and it can be awkward or painful. Two minutes of quiet can feel like a very long time.
  7. If you’re not sure if the interviewee is stuck or just thinking and quiet, ask them to explain what they’re thinking. This will help you avoid giving premature or unnecessary hints.
  8. If the interviewee is making progress, stay quiet. Sometimes it’s also hard to keep your mouth shut, and it can feel weird to sit there and observe in silence, but when the interviewee is excelling, the interviewer does very little talking!
  9. Take notes! Note things that go well and poorly so you can give feedback afterwards without interrupting the flow or atmosphere of the interview. Also write down how long the interviewee spends on each part (developing the initial algorithm, translating it into code, testing, etc) to understand where they struggle and excel.
  10. Encourage the interviewee to work through examples by hand and/or draw an illustration of the problem if they’re confused or stuck.
  11. Brainstorm “little hints”, “medium hints”, and “big hints” you can give if the interviewee gets stuck. “Little hints” tend to be open-ended (i.e., “how would you do this problem if you were solving it by hand?”) while “big hints” point the partner to the correct algorithm (i.e., “what would happen if you used data structure X instead of data structure Y?) While “medium hints” unsurprisingly are somewhere in the middle (for example, they might indicate the area in which you want to make a change without giving away the specific change, such as “is there another data structure you could use instead?”).
  12. If the interviewee is stuck, help them talk about their thoughts so far before giving a hint. Often talking through the problem will get an partner unstuck without any hints by acting as a “rubber duck.” Questions like “and then what?” or “what about when…?” without bringing in any new information are often sufficient to keep the ideas and words flowing.
  13. If you do have to give hints, give them one at a time, in increasing order of specificity (i.e., start with a “small hint” and only work up to a “big hint” if the interviewee is still stuck and running out of time). Leave plenty of space between the hints to give the interviewee time to work with them.
  14. Keep track of the time! When time is almost up, tell your partner you’re almost out of time, and ask them to wrap up their solution as best as possible, such as by explaining what they would do if they had more time. It helps you get a sense of how their thinking has progressed and creates a better experience for them.
  15. Stay in character until the interview is over! You’re the interviewer, not a peer or teacher. The best mocks are the ones that most closely replicate a true interview.
  16. After the interview ends, break your interviewer character and switch to peer/teacher mode. Leave enough time to give face-to-face constructive feedback. Give honest feedback so your partner can avoid repeating mistakes from mock interviews in real interviews! Not pointing out mistakes is not neutral - it actually encourages interviewees to repeat those mistakes. Include feedback on both technical skills and soft skills, and be sure to also point out what the interviewee did well so they know to keep doing it.

docs.text:
1. First Element Occurring K Times in an Array (Follow-Up: Last element occurring K times in array)
  2. Missing Elements in a Range

docs.title: First Element Occurring K Times in an Array
docs.text: Given an array and an integer k, return the first element that occurs k times.

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
For each element in the array, iterate through the array and count the number of occurrences. If it occurs k or more times, return the element, otherwise continue to the next element.

Complexity:

Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(1)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Keep a map of element counts. Iterate through the array, incrementing the count of each element in a map. If the count equals k, return the element.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

C++ Sample Code

#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

int firstKRepeats(vector<int> &vec, int k) {
    auto counts = unordered_map<int, int>();
    for (int x: vec) {
       counts[x]++;
       if (counts[x] == k)
           return x;
    }
    // Agree on a value to return here.
    // If you stipulate the values are positive, -1 works well.
    return -1;
}

docs.title: Follow-Up
docs.text:
What about if we wanted the last element occurring K times?

Instead of returning when we find an element that occurs k times, we can update a variable keeping track of the last time an element occurring k times was seen. Note that iterating backwards does not work, because an element that occurs more than k times may incorrectly be returned. Time and space complexity are the same as in the original problem.

docs.title: Missing Elements in a Range
docs.text: Given an array and two integers, lo and hi, defining a range, return the values in the range missing from the array.

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Sort the array, then perform a binary search for the low value. Traverse from where it is (or is not found) until the high value and store the missing numbers in an array. (Equivalently, search for the high value and traverse backwards to the low value.)

Complexity:

Time: O(nlogn)

Space: O(logn) or O(n) extra space, depending on the sorting algorithm; most built-in sorts are quicksort, which is O(logn). Also O(k) required space for the return value, where k is the size of the range.

docs.title: Almost Optimal
docs.text:
Iterate over the array, creating a set of the array elements. Iterate over the range, checking the set for the value at each iteration and adding it to an array if not present.

Complexity:

Time: O(n + k) or, equivalently, O(max(n, k))

Space: O(n) extra space. Also O(k) required space for the return value, where k is the size of the range.

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Iterate over the array, adding each element in the range to a set. Iterate over the range, checking the set for the value at each iteration and adding it to an array if not present.

Complexity:

Time: O(n + k) or, equivalently, O(max(n, k))

Space: O(min(n, k)) extra space. Also O(k) required space for the return value, where k is the size of the range.

C++ Sample Code

#include <unordered_set>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

vector<int> missingFromRange(vector<int> &vec, int lo, int hi) {
    auto present = unordered_set<int>();
    auto missing = vector<int>();
    for (int x: vec)
       if (x >= lo && x <= hi)
           present.insert(x);
    for (int i = lo; i <= hi; i++)
       if (present.count(i) == 0)
           missing.push_back(i);
    return missing;
}

docs.title: Pangrams
docs.text: A pangram is a phrase or sentence containing every letter (a-z) in the English alphabet. Given a string, determine if it is a pangram.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Input: “The quick brown fox jumps over the dog”

Output: False

Input: “The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog”

Output: True

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Convert the string to lowercase. Iterate over the lowercase alphabet and search the string for the letter. If the letter is not found, return false. If the end of the alphabet is reached, return true.

Complexity:

Time: O(n); O(n*m) where m is the size of the alphabet

Space: O(1)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Create an alphabet array of 0s of size 26. Convert the string to lowercase. Iterate over the string. Convert the current character to an integer and shift (so a-z are 0-25). If the integer representation is 0-25, set the value at that index to 1. Iterate over the alphabet array. If a 0 is encountered, return false. If the end of the array is reached, return true. (Equivalently, a set or map can be used.)

Complexity:

Time: O(n); O(n+m) where m is the size of the alphabet (considering the alphabet size as a constant, the brute force and optimal are the same; if the candidate codes the brute force solution and states this encourage them to think of a solution that scales for a larger alphabet)

Space: O(n)

C++ Sample Code

#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>

using namespace std;

bool is_pangram(string str) {
    lower = transform(str.begin(), str.end(), tolower);
    auto alpha = vector<bool>(26, False);
    for (char c: str) {
       int ascii_shift = c - 'a';
       if (ascii_shift >= 0 && ascii_shift < 26)
            alpha[ascii_shift] = True;
    }
    for (bool b: alpha)
       if (!b) return False
    return True;
}

docs.title: Isomorphic Strings
docs.text: Two strings are considered isomorphic if the characters in one string can be replaced to get the characters in the other string. No two distinct characters can be replaced by the same character, but a character can be replaced with itself.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Input: “egg”, “add”

Output: True

Input: “foo”, “bar”

Output: False

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Return false if the strings are of unequal length. Iterate over the length of the strings. For each index, iterate backwards in each string until the same character is found or the beginning is reached. If the previous occurrence of each character is not the same, return false. If the end of the strings are reached, return true. Note: many variations of the same solution exist.

Complexity:

Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(1)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Return false if the strings are of unequal length. Create two maps representing the mappings from string one to string two and vice versa. Iterate over the length of the strings. If the current characters are not in the maps keyed on the respective strings, add them with the character in the other string as the value. If one is in its map and not the other, return false. If they are both in the map, return false if they do not correspond, and continue if they do. Return true if the end of the strings are reached. Note: many variations of the same solution exist.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

C++ Sample Code

#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <unordered_map>

using namespace std;

bool are_isomorphic(string str1, string str2) {
     if (str1.size() != str2.size()) return False;
     auto map1 = unordered_map<char, char>();
     auto map2 = unordered_map<char,char>();
     for (int i = 0; i < str1.size(); i++) {
         if ((map1.find(str1[i]) == map1.end()) != (map2.find(str2[i]) == map2.end()))
              return False
         if((map1.find(str1[i]) == map1.end()) {
              map1[str1[i]] = str2[i];
              map2[str2[i]] = str1[i];
         } else if (map1[str1[i]] != str2[i] || map2[str2[i]] != str1[i])
              return False;
     }
     return True;
}

docs.title: Subarrays of Size K Containing Duplicates
docs.text: Given an array of integers and an integer k, return the number of unique subarrays of size k that contain duplicate elements.

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Create a count. Iterate through the array. For each index, iterate through the rest of the array until a duplicate is encountered. If the indices are k or fewer apart, increment the count.

Complexity:

Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(1)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Create a map of integers to integers. Add the first k elements to the map, incrementing their counts. Initialize a count of subarrays to zero if there are no duplicates in the first k elements and 1 otherwise. Iterate over the array until i + k is out-of-bounds. For each index i, decrement the count of the element at i in the map and increment the count of the element at i + k. Check the map for values greater than 1; if there are any, increment the count of subarrays.

Complexity:

Time: O(n) or O(n*k)

Space: O(1) or O(k)

C++ Sample Code

#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>

using namespace std;

int dupKSubArrays(vector<int> &vec, int k) {
    auto window = unordered_map<int>();
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) {
        window[vec[i]]++;
        if (window[vec[i]] > 1)
            count = 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < vec.size() - k; i++) {
        window[vec[i]]--;
        window[vec[i+k]]++;
        for (int element : window)
            if (element.second > 1) {
                count++;
                break;
           }
    }
    return count;
}

docs.title: Max Stock Profit with Single Buy/Sell
docs.text: Given an array of integers representing the price of a stock over time, return the maximum profit that can be made on a share by buying and selling at most once.

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Keep track of the max profit (initialized to zero) in a variable. Use a nested loop to check the profit at every possible buy/sell combination and compare to the max profit so far.

Complexity:

Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(1)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Use two variables to keep track of the max profit and the buy point (both initialized to zero). Iterate through the array. If the current value is less than the value at the buy point, update the buy point to the current index. Otherwise, compute the profit with the current index as the sell point and compare to the max profit so far.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

C++ Sample Code

#include <vector>

using namespace std;

int stockProfit(vector<int> &vec) {
    int profit = 0;
    int buy = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < vec.size(); i++)
        if (vec[i] < vec[buy])
             buy = i;
        else if (vec[i] - vec[buy] > profit) {
             profit = vec[i] - vec[buy];
    return profit;
}

docs.title: Follow-Up
docs.text:
What if we were allowed unlimited buys and sells?

Iterate over the array. If the next element is greater than the current element, add the difference to the profit.

docs.title: Number of Triplets with Zero Sum
docs.text: Given an array of integers, return the number of unique triplets that sum to zero.

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Keep a count of triplets. Use a triple nested loop to iterate through every possible triplet of indices and check whether the sum of the elements equals zero and if so, increment the count.

Complexity:

Time: O(n^3)

Space: O(1)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Create a map of integers to integers. Iterate through the array and increment the count of each element. Use a nested loop to iterate through every possible pair of indices. Calculate the target value by negating the sum of the two elements. If the target is in the map and the count of the target is greater than or equal to the occurrences of the target in the triplet, increment the count.

Complexity:

Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(n)

C++ Sample Code

#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>

using namespace std;

int tripletsZeroSum(vector<int> &vec) {
    auto counts = unordered_map<int>();
    int count = 0;
    for (int element : vec)
        counts[element]++;
    for (int i = 0; i < vec.size(); i++)
        for (int j = i+1; j < vec.size(); j++) {
            int target = -1 * (vec[i] + vec[j]);
           if (counts.find(target) == counts.end())
               continue;
           if (vec[i] == target && vec[j] == target && counts[target] < 3)
               continue;
           if (vec[i] == target || vec[j] == target && counts[target] < 2)
               Continue;
           count++;
        }
    return count;
}

docs.title: Follow-Up
docs.text:
What about if we wanted the number of triplets summing to any given target?

Pass the target sum to the function and calculate the value to lookup in the map by subtracting the sum of the pair from that value.

docs.title: Max Meetings in a Room
docs.text: Given an array of numeric pairs representing the start and end times of scheduled meetings, find the maximum number of meetings that can be held in a room if only one meeting can occur in the room at once.

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Check if any of the meetings overlap. If not, return the number of meetings. Otherwise, try removing each of the overlapping meetings and repeat.

Complexity:

Time: O(n!) (Do not even let the candidate code this solution.)

Space: O(1)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Sort the meetings by end time. Initialize a count to one and index (to track the last selected meeting) to 0. Iterate through the meetings starting at index 1. If the last selected meeting’s end time is less than or equal to the current meeting’s start time, the meeting can be held in the same room; increment the count and update the index to the current index.

Complexity:

Time: O(nlogn)

Space: O(1)

C++ Sample Code

#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>

using namespace std;

int maxMeetingsRoom(vector<pair<float, float>> &vec) {
    if (!vec.size())
       return 0;
    sort(vec.begin(), vec.end(), [](const pair<int, int> &left, const pair<int, int> &right) {
        if (left.second != right.second)
            return left.second < right.second;
        else
            return left.first < right.first;
    });
    int count = 1;
    int ind = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i < vec.size(); i++)
        if (vec[i].first >= vec[ind].second) {
            count++;
            ind = i;
        }
    return count;
}
