docs.title: Reverse Linked List in Groups of k
docs.text: Given the head node of a linked list, reverse the linked list in groups of k.

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Iterate over the linked list and copy it to a temporary array. Iterate over the array using the indices to reverse the elements in groups of k. (One optimal variation of this is to use nested loops with an outer loop that increments i by k, rather than the typical 1, and an inner loop that iterates only over i to i +k, reversing the elements.) Iterate over the linked list again, overwriting the data with the corresponding element in the array.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

docs.title: Good
docs.text:
Reverse the first k elements recursively using a counter for k. Recurse on the remainder of the list, setting element k’s next to the result.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n/k) (O(1) explicit, O(n/k) implicit recursive stack space)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Reverse the first k elements iteratively using a counter for k. Recurse on the remainder of the list, setting element k’s next to the result.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

C++ Sample Code

using namespace std;

Node *kReverse(Node *head, int k) {
    int count = 0;
    Node *curr = head;
    Node *next = nullptr;
    Node *prev = nullptr;
    Node *newHead = nullptr;
    Node *newTail = nullptr;
    Node *tail = nullptr;
    while (curr) {
        count = k;
        join = curr;
        prev = nullptr;
        while (curr && count--) {
            next = curr->next;
            curr->next = prev;
            prev = curr;
            curr = next;
        }
        if (!newHead)
             newHead = prev;
        if (tail)
             tail->next = prev;
        tail = newTail;
    }
    return newHead;
}

docs.title: Max Height of a Binary Tree
docs.text: Given a binary tree, find the longest path from the root to a leaf (node with no children).

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Use any traversal to find every leaf node. Then use any traversal to find the distance to each leaf node. Return the maximum.

Complexity

Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(n)

Note: do not let the candidate code this solution!

docs.title: Good
docs.text:
Use a post-order traversal to calculate the heights of the left and right subtrees and return the max plus one.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n) (O(1) explicit, O(n) implicit stack space)

docs.title: Good
docs.text:
Use a level-order traversal using either two queues for current and previous level or pushing null values (if permitted in the language of choice) to mark the end of levels. If the former, keep a level count that is incremented every time the current level is reset; if the latter, keep a level count that is incremented whenever a null value is popped.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
The Morris traversal algorithm makes this possible in O(1) space. It is not expected that candidates will find this solution; therefore the sample solution below is a “good” solution.

C++ Sample Code

#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int maxDepth(Node *root) {
    if (!root)
        return 0;
    return 1 + max(maxDepth(root->left), maxDepth(root->right));
}

docs.title: Number of Nodes within K Distance of Root
docs.text: Given a binary tree, count the number of nodes within k distance of the root.

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Use any traversal to find every node. Then use any traversal to find the depth of each node. Count the number of values less than or equal to k.

Complexity

Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(n)

Note: do not let the candidate code this solution!

docs.title: Better
docs.text:
Use a level-order or pre-order traversal to find the depth of each node. Count the number of values less than or equal to k.

Complexity

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

Note: do not let the candidate code this solution!

docs.title: Good
docs.text:
Use a level-order traversal using either two queues for current and previous level. Keep two counts: a level count that is incremented every time the current level is reset; and a node count that is incremented every time a node is popped. When the level count exceeds k, return the node count.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

Note that while Big O space and time are the same as the “Better” solution, because this solution terminates early, in practice it is much better.

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Use a pre-order traversal that accepts the distance from the root and k. Increment the distance; if it is greater than k, return 0; otherwise return one plus the counts from the left and right subtrees.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(k) (O(1) explicit, O(k) implicit stack space)

Note: in the worst case (k=n), the max space for the “Good” solution is n/2 and the max space for the “Optimal” solution is n, since we typically consider k \<\< n, the solutions are labelled this way. However, both are acceptable. If the candidate considers and weighs this, that is the ideal, although not expected.

C++ Sample Code

#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int countWithinK(Node *root, int k, int depth) {
    if (!root || depth+1 > k)
        return 0;
    return 1 + countWithinK(root->left, k, depth+1), countWithinK(root->right, k, depth+1));
}

int countWithinK(Node *root, int k) {
    return countWithinK(root, k, 0);
}

docs.title: Median of a Sorted Linked List
docs.text: Given a sorted singly list of integers, return the median value.

docs.title: Brute Force
docs.text:
Copy the linked list into an array and use the indices to find the median.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

Note: do not let the candidate code this solution!

docs.title: Good
docs.text:
Iterate over the list to find its length. Then iterate again to find the middle(s).

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

docs.title: Optimal
docs.text:
Use fast-slow pointers to find the middle(s) at the same time as the length.

Complexity:

Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

Note: the Big O is the same as the “Good” solution but a traversal is eliminated, making this the better solution.

C++ Sample Code

using namespace std;

Node *median(Node *head) {
    Node *slow = head;
    Node *fast = head;
    int count = 0;
    while (fast) {
        count++;
        fast = fast->next;
        if (fast) {
            count++;
            fast = fast->next;
            if (fast->next)
                slow = slow->next;
        }
    }
    if (count % 2)
        return slow->next->value;
    return (slow->value + slow->next->value) / 2;
}

docs.title: Question 1: Zero Sum
docs.text:
Given an array of integers, return the number of pairs of integers in the array that sum to 0 assuming you can use the element at each index at most once.

Technique: Hash the counts

Approach: Iterate over the array, building a map of integers to counts. Initialize a final count to zero. Iterate over the map. Do one of the following:

  1. For each negative (or positive) integer, do nothing. For each positive (or negative) integer x, look up the count of x*-1. Add the minimum of the counts of x and x*-1 to the final count. If 0 is encountered, divide the count by 2 (rounded down) and add it to the final count.
  2. Look up the count of x*1. Add the minimum of the counts of x and x*-1 to the final count. When the iteration is complete, divide the final count by 2 (rounded down) before returning it.

Follow-Up: Given an array of integers, return the number of pairs of integers in the array that sum

Big O: O(n) space, O(n) time

docs.title: Follow-Up
docs.text:
Now assume you can re-use elements in different pairs (i.e., the elements in a pair must be from different indices but different pairs may use an element form the same index).

Technique: Hash the counts

Approach: Iterate over the array, building a map of integers to counts. Initialize a final count to zero. Iterate over the map. Do one of the following:

  1. For each negative (or positive) integer, do nothing. For each positive (or negative) integer x, look up the count of x*-1. Add the product of the counts of x and x*-1 to the final count. If 0 is encountered with count y, add the product of y and (y-1)/2 to the final count.
  2. Look up the count of x*1. Add the product of the counts of x and x*-1 to the final count. When the iteration is complete, divide the final count by 2 before returning it.

Big O: O(n) space, O(n) time

docs.title: Question 2: Unique Sum
docs.text:
Given an array of integers, return the sum of unique elements in the array.

Technique: Hash the elements

Approach:

Do one of the following:

  1. Iterate over the array, building a set of the elements (or, equivalently, initializing a set from the array if supported in the language of choice, or building a map with garbage/identical values if the language of choice does not have a built-in set data structure). Initialize a final count. Iterate over the set, adding each element to the final count.
  2. Initialize a final count. Iterate over the array, building a set of the elements (or, equivalently, building a map with garbage/identical values if the language of choice does not have a built-in set data structure). Before adding an element to the set, check if it is already present; if it is not, add it to the final count.

Big O: O(n) space, O(n) time

docs.title: Question 3: First Occurrence
docs.text:
Given a string, return a string that contains only the first occurrence of each character in the string.

Technique: Hash the elements

Approach:

Initialize a result string. Iterate over the string, building a set of the characters (or, equivalently, building a map with garbage/identical values if the language of choice does not have a built-in set data structure). Before adding a character to the set, check if it is already present; if it is not, append it to the result string.

Note: the solution should avoid O(n) string appends (if possible in the language of choice) as that would result in a time complexity of O(n^2). The technique for doing so depends on the mutability of strings and the options for initialization in the language of choice. In a language with mutable strings, this could involve allocating a result string the same size as the original string, then truncating it to the size of the set. In a language with immutable strings that allows string initialization from an array, this could involve building the result as an array of characters and initializing the result string only at the end.

Big O: O(n) space, O(n) time

Instructions
docs.text:
Before beginning this section, read up on the definitions of Big O notation, time and space complexity, hashing, and set and map data structures if they are unfamiliar to you or you need a refresher.

  1. Big O Notation
  2. Time Complexity
  3. Time vs. Space Complexity
  4. Asymptotic Notations
  5. Sets and Maps
  6. Hashing and Maps

In your technical interview for entrance into the UCP cohort, you were asked a question in which you were given an array or a string. Most array and string problems can be solved in O(n^2) time using nested loops; this is the “brute force” solution. However, most of these solutions can be improved to O(n) time. Over the course of homeworks 0 and 1 and workshop 1, we will be exploring techniques for doing so.

Using hash data structures (sets or maps) is one such technique. To use this technique, iterate over the array or string and hash each element, then iterate over the hash data structure to get the solution. This is an example of a time-space trade-off; in most cases, using this technique will increase the space from O(1) to O(n) to achieve optimal time complexity of O(n). What you store in your hash data structure depends on the problem. There are three main variations. From simplest to most complex:

  1. Hash the elements. Use a hash set (or a hash map in which the values do not matter if your language does not support sets) and just hash the elements themselves. This is equivalent to converting the array or string to a set. Use this technique if the solution requires knowing about the presence or absence of elements.
  2. Hash the counts. Use a hash map and iterate through the array or string, adding each element to the map with a count of 1 if not present and incrementing the count if present. The result is a hash map representing the occurrences of each element in the original array or string. Use this technique if the solution requires knowing about the frequency of elements.
  3. Compute and hash something else. Sometimes the solution will require a different value per element. For example, this could be the index of the element in the original data structure or a value computed based on other elements in the data structure. In this case, use a hash map, do any precomputation that requires iterating through the initial data structure first (if necessary), then iterate through the array or string computing and storing the value for each element.

In most cases, the required solution will not be in the form of a set or map but rather require you to look up or compute something based on your set or map.

You will now do three array/string problems that can be optimally solved in O(n) time and O(n) space using a hash data structure and one of these three techniques. For each problem, write a function to solve the problem and write test cases to check your function. When run, the file you submit should execute your function on your test cases (e.g., through a main method, if applicable in your language). docs.title: Question 1: Max Mean Sub Array
docs.text:
Given an array of integers and an integer, k, find the maximum mean of a subarray of size k.

Technique: Fixed-size sliding window

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see MaxMeanSubArray.

  1. Create an auxiliary sums array of the same size as the original, or, equivalently, a map of indices to integers. Iterate through the array; for index i, store the sum of the element at i plus the sum at i-1 in the auxiliary array at index i in the sums array (in other words, each index i in the sums array represents the sum from index 0 to index i). Initialize a max sum variable to sums[k-1]. Starting at index k, iterate through the sums array, for each index i comparing the difference sums[i] - sums[i-k] to the max sum and updating it when appropriate.
  2. Compute the sum of the first k elements (indices 0 through k-1). Initialize a max sum variable to this sum. Iterate over the array starting at index k. For each index i, subtract the element at i-k from the sum and add the element at i. Compare the max sum to the new sum and update it when appropriate.

Big O: O(n) time, O(n) space (approach 1) or O(1) space (approach 2)

docs.title: Question 2: Reverse Vowels
docs.text:
Given a string, reverse the order of the vowels in the string.

Technique: Forward-backward two-pointer

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see ReverseVowels.

Initialize a forward pointer to index 0 and a backward pointer to index n-1 where n is the length of the string. While the forward index is less than the backward index, repeat the following steps:

  1. Advance the forward index until it is on a vowel.
  2. Advance the backwards index until it is on a vowel.
  3. Swap the elements at the forward and backwards indices.
  4. Increment the forward index.
  5. Decrement the backwards index.

Big O: O(n) time, O(1) space

docs.title: Question 3: Zero Sum Sub Arrays
docs.text:
Given an array of integers, count the number of subarrays that sum to zero.

Technique: Hash the running computation

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see ZeroSumSubArrays. (Note: linked write-up asks to print all subarrays with void output; we ask to return the number of subarrays with no printing.)

Initialize a map of sums to counts. Initialize a running sum to zero. Initialize a count of arrays to zero. Iterate through the array, adding the current element to the running sum. Check if the running sum is already in the map. If so, add the current value for the running sum to the count of arrays, then increment the value. Otherwise, add the sum to the map with a value of one.

Big O: O(n) time, O(n) space

docs.title: Question 4: Backspace String Compare
docs.text:
Given two strings representing series of keystrokes, determine whether the resulting text is the same. Backspaces are represented by the '#' character so "x#" results in the empty string ("").

Technique: Simultaneous iteration two-pointer

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see BackspaceStringCompare.

Initialize two pointers, one in each string, to the last index. While the two pointers are both greater than or equal to zero, repeat the following steps:

  1. If the characters at the two pointers are the same and not #, decrement both pointers.
  2. If the characters at the two pointers are different and neither is #, return false.
  3. If either or both characters are #, decrement that pointer until the next character is not #, keeping a count k of the # characters encountered. While k is not 0, repeat the following:
    1. Decrement the pointer.
    2. If the current character is not #, decrement k.

If both pointers are -1, return true. Otherwise, return false.

Big O: O(n) time, O(1) space

docs.title: Question 5: Shortest Substring
docs.text:
Given a string and a second string representing required characters, return the length of the shortest substring containing all the required characters.

Technique: Growing/shrinking sliding window

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see ShortestSubstring.

Initialize a map of characters to counts. Initialize start and end indices and a character count to infinity (max int). Convert the string of required characters to a set. Increment the end index, checking if the at that index character to see if it is in the required set. If it is, increment its count in the map (or add it to the map with a count of one if not already present). When the size of the map equals the size of the required set, set the character count to the length of the string between the start and end indices, inclusive. Stop incrementing the end index, and increment the start index, checking if the at that index character to see if it is in the required set. If it is, decrement its count in the map (or remove it if its count is one). When the size of the map is no longer the size of the required set, set the character count to the length of the string between the start and end indices plus one, inclusive. Stop incrementing the start index, and repeat the process until the string is exhausted.

Big O: O(n) time, O(n) space

docs.title: Question 6: Missing Integer
docs.text:
Given an integer n and a sorted array of integers of size n-1 which contains all but one of the integers in the range 1-n, find the missing integer.

Technique: Binary search variation

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see MissingInteger.

Perform a binary search the with following conditions:

  1. Missing integer found: the difference between the current element and the previous element is two rather than one. Return the integer between the two elements.
  2. Reduce search space to the left half of the array (decrease upper bound): the difference between the current (middle) element and its index is two.
  3. Reduce search space to right half of array (increase lower bound): the difference between the current (middle) element and its index is one.

Big O: O(logn) time, O(1) space

docs.title: Question 7: K Anagrams
docs.text:
Two strings are considered to be “k-anagrams” if they can be made into anagrams by changing at most k characters in one of the strings. Given two strings and an integer k, determine if they are k-anagrams.

Technique: Increment/decrement counts

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see KAnagrams.

Return false if the strings are not the same length. Initialize a map of characters to counts. Iterate through one string, increasing the count of each character encountered. Iterate through the second string, decreasing the count of each character encountered. Initialize a count of differences to zero. Iterate through the values in the map, adding the absolute value of every value to the difference count. Return true if the final difference count is less than or equal to k and false otherwise.

Big O: O(n) time, O(n) space

docs.title: Question 8: Merge Intervals
docs.text:
Given a list of integer pairs representing the low and high end of an interval, inclusive, return a list in which overlapping intervals are merged.

Technique: Sort, then solve

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see MergeIntervals.

Initialize a list of merged intervals. Sort the pairs by the first value (start of the interval). Initialize a start value to the start of the first interval. Repeat the following steps until the list is exhausted:

  1. If there is no next interval, add the saved start value and end value of the current interval to the merged list.
  2. If the end of the next interval is greater than the end of the current interval, add the saved start value and end value of the current interval to the merged list. Move to the next interval and reset the start value to its start.
  3. If the end of the next interval is less than or equal to the end of the current interval, move to the next interval without resetting the start value.

(Equivalently, you can sort by the second value, or end of the interval, and iterate backwards starting at the last interval, checking whether the end of the the previous interval is less than the start of the current interval.)

Big O: O(nlogn) time, O(1), O(logn), or O(n) space for sorting depending on the algorithm, O(n) for return value

docs.title: Question 9: Dedup Array
docs.text:
Given a sorted array of non-negative integers, modify the array by removing duplicates so each element only appears once. If arrays are static (aka, not dynamic/resizable) in your language of choice, the remaining elements should appear in the left-hand side of the array and the extra space in the right-hand side should be padded with -1s.

Technique: Two-pointer with “catch-up” condition

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see DedupArray. Initialize a leading and trailing pointer to 0. Increment the leading pointer; if the element at that index is not the same as the previous element, increment the trailing pointer and set the element at its index to the element at the leading index. Repeat until the leading pointer reaches the final index; increment the trailing pointer and set it to the last element. The final position of the trailing pointer indicates the end of the updated array.

Big O: O(n) time, O(1) space

docs.title: Question 7: Copy Tree
docs.text:
Given a binary tree, create a deep copy. Return the root of the new tree.

Technique: Pre-order traversal.

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see CopyTree. (Note: the linked solution is to clone a binary tree with random pointers; we asked just to clone a binary tree so only the “copyLeftRightNode” portion of the solution is needed.)

Implement a pre-order traversal with the following steps:

  1. If the current node is null return null.
  2. Make a copy of the current node.
  3. Recursively call the pre-order traversal on the left child and set the copy’s left child to the result.
  4. Recursively call the pre-order traversal on the right child and set the copy’s right child to the result.

Call the traversal on the root of the tree and return the result.

Big O: O(n) time, O(n) space

docs.title: Question 8: Is BST
docs.text:
Technique: Generic depth-first traversal or level-order traversal.

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see IsBST.

Approach 1:

Implement any depth-first traversal with the following conditions:

  1. If the current node is null or has no children, return false.
  2. If the current node has a left child and it is greater than the node, return false.
  3. If the current node has a right child and it is less than the node, return false.
  1. Recursively call the traversal on the left child and the right child. Return true if both true, false otherwise.

Call the traversal on the root of the tree and return the result.

Approach 2:

Implement a level-order traversal that stores the result in an array. Call the traversal, then iterate through the resulting array, checking if it is sorted. Return true if sorted, false otherwise.

Big O: O(n) time, O(logn) space (approach 1) or O(n) space (approach 2)

docs.title: Question 9: Dedup Sorted List
docs.text:
Technique: Linked list reset/catch-up two-pointer

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see DedupSortedList.

Initialize a leading and a trailing pointer to the head of the list. While there is a next node and the data in the next node is the same as the data in the current node, advance the leading pointer. Set the trailing pointer’s next node to the leading pointer’s next node. Reset both pointers to the next node. Continue until the list is exhausted. Return the head.

Big O: O(n) time, O(1) space

docs.title: Question 10: Move Nth Last to Front
docs.text:
Technique: Linked list fixed-distance two-pointer

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see MoveNthLastToFront (Note: the linked solution is to delete the nth to last node but we asked them to move it to the front. The algorithm for finding the nth to last node and re-linking the adjacent nodes is the same; their solution should just have the additional step of updating the head.)

Initialize a leading and a trailing pointer to the head of the list. Advance the leading pointer n times. Advance both pointers until the leading pointer is the tail (its next pointer is null). Save the trailing pointer’s next as the new head. Set the trailing pointer’s next to the new head’s next. Set the new head’s next to the head and return the new head.

Big O: O(n) time, O(1) space

docs.title: Question 11: Is Palindrome
docs.text:
Technique: Doubly linked list forward-backward two-pointer

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see IsPalindrome.

Find the tail of the list. Initialize a forward pointer to the head of the list and a backward pointer to the tail of the list. Compare the data at the two pointers. If it is the same, move both pointers. If it is different, return false. If the pointers are the same or the forward pointer’s previous is the backwards pointer (or, equivalent, the backward pointer’s next is the previous pointer), return true. Repeat.

Big O: O(n) time, O(1) space

docs.title: Question 12: Disconnect Cycle
docs.text:
Technique: Hash linked list nodes

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see DisconnectCycle.

Initialize a set of node pointers. Add the head of the list to the set. Initialize a current pointer to the head. While its next pointer is not in the set, add it to the set and advance the pointer. If the next pointer is in the set, set the next pointer to null. Return the head.

Big O: O(n) time, O(n) space

docs.title: Question 13: Left View

Technique: Level-order (breadth-first) traversal

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see LeftView. (Note: the linked solution is to print the left view. We are asking them to return an array containing the left view.)

Initialize an array representing the left view. Conduct a level order traversal using two queues for the current level and the next level. Whenever the current level is reset (i.e., the root is added or the current level is set to the next level), add the first node in the queue to the left view array. When the traversal is completed, return the array.

Big O: O(n) time, O(n) space

docs.title: Question 14: Floor in BST

Technique: Search BST

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see FloorInBst.

Initialize floor to the value that will be returned if there is no floor in the tree. Search the tree for the value. Every time the value you are searching for is greater than the current node (i.e., you will update current to be its right child), set the return value to the current node. If the value is found, return the value. Otherwise, return the saved floor value when current is null (the value is not found).

Big O: O(logn) time, O(1) space

docs.title: Question 4: Queue (20 min max)
docs.text:
Queues are not a “first-class” data structure – they are an API or interface implemented using another underlying data structure. Queues should have O(1) insertion and deletion; because insertion and deletion occur at opposite ends, the underlying data structure is normally a linked list to satisfy this requirement. Implement a queue class according to the following definition; you may copy-paste and reuse any parts of your solution to Question 1 or 2. Again, for simplicity, you can make your queue store integers rather than generic data types. Queues are necessary auxiliary data structures to implement breadth-first traversals of graphs and trees. For those problems, you should use your language’s built-in; we are asking you to implement a queue here for two reasons: to demonstrate one of the use cases of linked lists and to give you an understanding of how they work.

class Queue {
    int peek() // returns the first item in the queue. O(1) time.
    void enqueue(int x) // adds x to the back of the queue. O(1) time.
    int dequeue() // removes and returns the first item in the queue. O(1) time.
    bool isEmpty() // returns a boolean indicating whether the queue is empty. O(1) time.
}

docs.title: Question 5: Stack (20 min max)
docs.text:
Stacks are also not a “first-class” data structure and should also have O(1) insertion and deletion. Because insertion and deletion occur at the same end, this can be achieved with either an array or a linked list. Implement a queue class according to the following definition using a linked list as the underlying data structure; you may copy-paste and reuse any parts of your solution to Question 1 or 2. Again, for simplicity, you can make your stack store integers rather than generic data types. You will likely implement your depth-first traversals of graphs and trees recursively; however, if you chose to do them iteratively, you would need to use a stack.

class Stack {
    int top() // returns the top item in the stack. O(1) time.
    void push(int x) // adds x to the top of the stack. O(1) time.
    int pop() // removes and returns the top item in the stack. O(1) time.
    bool isEmpty() // returns a boolean indicating whether the stack is empty. O(1) time.
}

docs.title: Question 6: Deque (20 min max)
docs.text:
Finally, dequeues (short for double-ended queues) are another “non-first-class” data structure that have the features of both stacks and queues: O(1) insertion and deletion at both ends. Implement a deque class according to the following definition; you may copy-paste and reuse any parts of your solution to Question 1 or 2. As usual, for simplicity, you can make your dequeue store integers rather than generic data types.

class Deque {
    int front() // returns the first item in the deque. O(1) time.
    int back() // returns the last item in the deque. O(1) time.
    void pushBack(int x) // adds x to the back of the deque. O(1) time.
    void pushFront(int x) // adds x to the front of the deque. O(1) time.
    int popFront() // removes and returns the first item in the deque. O(1) time.
    int popBack() // removes and returns the last item in the deque. O(1) time.
    bool isEmpty() // returns a boolean indicating whether the deque is empty. O(1) time.
}

docs.title: Question 2: Build a Heap
docs.text:
Approach:

Store the heap in an array where the parent of the node at i is located at (i-1)/2 and the children are located at (2*i)+1 and (2*i)+2. The root is located at index 0. To add an element, insert at the end of the array and “bubble it up” until it reaches the correct position (i.e., compare it to its parent, and if they are out of order, swap them). To delete the root, swap it with the last element, then “heapify” it (i.e., find the correct parent between it and its two children; if it is not the root, swap it, and repeat on the swapped child). For a full write-up and sample code see binary heap.

docs.title: Question 3: Build a Priority Queue
docs.text:
Approach:

Use a max heap and store a pair of data and a priority (integer) in each location. Use the priority for all comparisons. For a full write-up and sample code see priority queue.

docs.title: Question 4: Number of Islands
docs.text:
Given a binary matrix in which 1s represent land and 0s represent water, return the number of islands (contiguous 1s surrounded by 0s or the edge of the matrix).

Technique: Graph, generic traversal

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see BFS solution or DFS solution.

Initialize an island count to zero. Conduct either a BFS or DFS traversal starting with an arbitrary node (i.e., location on the grid); choose a corner for simplicity and traverse rows or columns with two nested loops. Every time the search is started with a new, previously unvisited node, increment the island count. When the search is exhausted (the number of visited nodes is the same as the number of locations in the grid), return the count.

Big O: O(n) time, O(n) space

docs.title: Question 5: First K Binary Numbers
docs.text:
Given a number, k, return an array of the first k binary numbers, represented as strings.

Technique: Queue

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see FirstKBinaryNumbers. (Note: the linked solution starts with “1” as the first binary number but we are asking them to start with “0”. This is a special case because we do not wish to put “0” in the queue and append to it since none of the other numbers start with “0”.)

Initalize a result array with the string “0”. Initalize a count to 1. Initalize a queue and push “1” to the queue. While the count is less than k, add the front of the queue, s, to the array, push s + “0” and s + “1” to the queue, and pop the queue. Increment the count. When the count equals k, return the array.

Big O: O(n) time, O(n) space

docs.text:

Given a list of towns and a list of pairs representing roads between towns, return the number of road networks. (For example, a state in which all towns are connected by roads has 1 road network, and a state in which none of the towns are connected by roads has 0 road networks.)

Technique: Graph, generic traversal

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see RoadNetworks. (Note: this is a word problem version of finding the number of connected components in an undirected graph, which is the problem the linked solution is for.)

Initalize a network count to zero. Conduct either a BFS or DFS traversal starting with an arbitrary node (i.e., town); iterate over the list of towns for simplicity. Every time the search is started with a new, previously unvisisted node, incremement the network count. When the search is exhuasted (the number of visited nodes is the same as the number of nodes), return the count.

Big O: O(n) time, O(n) space

docs.title: Question 7: Reverse Words
docs.text:
Given a string, return the string with the order of the space-separated words reversed.

Technique: Stack

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see ReverseWords.

Initalize a temporary string, a result string, and a stack. Iterate through the input string, adding each character to the temporary string until a space is reached. Add the temporary string to the stack, then reset it to the empty string. Repeat until the input string is exhuasted, ending by pushing whatever remains in the temporary string (if not empty) to the stack. Then pop the stack, adding each word followed by a space (skipping the space when the stack is empty) to the result string. Return the result string.

Big O: O(n) time, O(n) space

docs.text:
Given an origin and a destination in a directed graph in which edges can be blue or red, determine the length of the shortest path from the origin to the destination in which the edges traversed alternate in color. Return -1 if no such path exists.

Technique: Graph, BFS

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see AlternatingPath.

Run a BFS from the origin to find the destination. Keep track of the color of the previous edge and explore only edges of the opposite color (for example, by using pairs in the queue to store both the node and the previous edge color). Also keep track of the length of the path (either by using a triple in the queue, or by using two queues and incrementing a count every time one queue is emptied, indicating we are moving a node further from the origin in the BFS).

docs.title: Question 9: Merge K Sorted Arrays
docs.text:
Given an array of k sorted arrays, merge the k arrays into a single sorted array.

Technique: Min heap

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see MergeKSortedArrays.

Initalize a min heap. Initalize a result array. Initialize an index in each array to 0. Add the elements at those indices to the heap. While the heap is not empty, repeat the following steps:

  1. Add the top element of the heap to the result.
  2. Increment the index for the array the top element came from. If it is still in bounds, add that element to the heap.
  3. Remove the top element from the heap.

Return the result array.

Big O: O(n) time, O(1) extra space, O(n) space for return value

docs.title: Question 11: Vacation Destinations
docs.text:
Given an origin city, a maximum travel time k, and pairs of destinations that can be reached directly from each other with corresponding travel times in hours, return the number of destinations within k hours of the origin. Assume that having a stopover in a city adds an hour of travel time.

Technique: Graph, DFS

Approach: This problem is equivalent to count nodes within k distance of source in a weighted graph with one additional step: incrementing the total path weight by one for each node after the source. Branches can be trimmed (i.e., recursion terminated) once the total path weight exceeds k.

Perform a DFS from the origin city. Have the recursive call accept a set of destinations and a distance. Make the initial call with an empty set and a distance of zero. If the distance from the current node to a neighbor plus one (if the current node isn’t the origin) plus the distance so far is less than k, make the recursive call to that neighbor with this value as the new distance and adding the neighbor to the set. When the recursion terminates, return the set.

Big O: O(n) time, O(n) space

docs.title: Question 1: Build a Trie
docs.text:
Implement a trie class, including the insert, search, and delete methods. Your class should adhere to the following API, adjusted appropriately for your language of choice.

Approach:

Insert: Traverse the word in parallel with the trie. For each letter, look up the corresponding location in the current node’s array. If it does not already contain a node, create one. When the end of the word is reached, mark the current node as a valid word.

Remove: Traverse the word in parallel with the trie. For each letter, look up the corresponding location in the current node’s array. When the end of the word is reached, un-mark the current node as a valid word. An improvement is to store the traversed nodes in a stack; once the end of the word is reached, if it has no children, remove it from its parent (the top node on the stack). Then pop the stack and repeat, also checking to ensure the node isn’t a valid word. Return once a node that is a valid word or has children is reached or the entire stack is popped.

Is Valid Word: Traverse the word in parallel with the trie. For each letter, look up the corresponding location in the current node’s array. If it does not already contain a node, return false. If the end of the word is reached, return the valid word marker at the terminal node.

docs.title: Question 2: Boggle
docs.text:
Boggle is a word game in which players compete to find the most words on a square grid of random letters. Valid words must be at least three characters and formed from non-overlapping (i.e., a position on the board can only be used once in a word) adjacent (including diagonal) letters. Given a Boggle board and a dictionary of valid words, return all valid words on the board.

Technique: Trie as a parameter

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see Boggle.

Accept the dictionary as a trie. Initialize a set of words. Use a nested loop to iterate through the Boggle board (matrix), using each as a starting letter. For each starting letter, initialize a visited set to contain the starting location and a current word to the starting letter. Perform a DFS from the starting node, adding each visited letter to the visited set and current word before making the recursive call. Traverse the trie in parallel; if the current word corresponds to a valid word, add it to the word set; if it is not on an existing path in the trie, return early. Reset the current word and visited set before performing the next DFS. Return the word set.

Big O: O(2^n) time (this is is still the upper bound, or worst case, but in practice using the trie dramatically improves this because very few letter combinations are valid word prefixes), O(n) space

docs.title: Question 3: Running Median
docs.text:
You are given an array of numbers representing a stream received one by one. Return an array representing the median after each new number is received.

Technique: Maintain two heaps

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see RunningMedian.

Initialize a min heap, a max heap, an array of medians, a current median to 0. Iterate through the input array. For each element is received, do the following:

  1. If the element is greater than the current median, add it to the min heap. Otherwise, add it to the max heap.
  2. If the size of the heaps differs by more than one, remove the top element from the larger heap and add it to the smaller heap.
  3. If the heaps are the same size, the current median is the mean of the tops of the heaps. Otherwise, the median is the top of the larger heap. Add the current median to the array and update the median element.

Return the array of medians.

Big O: O(nlogn) time, O(n) space

docs.title: Question 4: Catalan Numbers
docs.text:
The Catalan numbers are a mathematical sequence of numbers. The nth Catalan number is defined as (2n)! / (n+1)!n!. Given a non-negative integer n, return the Catalan numbers 0-n.

Technique: Dynamic programming; either tabulation or memoization works but tabulation is slightly preferable because it lacks the recursive overhead

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see CatalanNumbers.

Approach 1: Initialize an array of size n+1. Set the indices 0 and 1 to have the value 1 (the 0th and first Catalan numbers are one). Iterate from 2 to n, inclusive, to find the value for each index, i, in this range. In an inner loop, increment j from 0 to i, exclusive; add the product of the the values at indices j and i - j -1 to the value for i. Return the array.

Approach 2: This approach requires the mathematical observation that the formula for the nth Catalan number can be simplified to the product of the (n-1)th Catalan number and (4n - 2) / (n + 1). We don’t expect this approach. Iterate from 2 to n, inclusive, calculating each number based on the previous one.

Big O: O(n^2) time, O(n) space (approach 1); O(n) time, O(1) extra space, O(n) space for return value (approach 2)

docs.title: Question 5: Min Cost Stair Climbing
docs.text:
A staircase on a hiking trail implements a rather unusual toll system to cover trail maintenance costs. Each stair in the staircase has a different toll which you only have to pay if you step on that stair. Due to the height of the stairs, you can only climb one or two stairs at once. This means that from the ground you must initially step on either stair 0 or stair 1 and that, if there are n stairs, the last stair you step on can be either stair n-1 or n-2. Given an array representing the costs per stair, what is the minimum possible toll you can pay to climb the staircase?

Technique: Dynamic programming; either tabulation or memoization works but tabulation is slightly preferable because it lacks the recursive overhead

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see MinCostStairClimbing.

Approach 1: Initialize a min cost array of size n+1. Set the min cost for stairs 0 and 1 to their costs. Iterate to calculate the min cost for each index i from 2 to n, setting the min cost at i to the cost for i and plus the minimum of the costs for i - 1 and i -2. Return the value at index n.

Approach 2: Use two variables for the previous two indices (stairs) rather than an array.

Big O: O(n) time, O(n) space (approach 1); O(n) time, O(1) space

  1. If the current word is a valid word in the trie, if the next index has not already been visited, recurse with it as the start of the string. . When a valid word is found, recurse on the remainder of the string. If the next character is ever not

Big(O): O(n*m) time where m is the longest word in the dictionary, O(n) space

docs.title: Question 7: Largest Square of 1s
docs.text:
Given a square matrix of 0s and 1s, find the dimension of the largest square consisting only of 1s.

Technique: Dynamic programming; either tabulation or memoization works but tabulation is slightly preferable because it lacks the recursive overhead

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see LargestSquareOf1s.

Create a DP matrix of the same size as the original. Copy the first row and first column. Use two nested loop to iterate through the rest of the matrix. For each location, if the element is 0, set the DP value to 0. Otherwise, set the DP value to setting each location DP[i][j] to one plus the minimum of DP[i][j-1] and DP[i-1][j]. Iterate through the DP matrix and find the maximum value. Return it.

Big O: O(n*m) time, O(n*m) space

docs.title: Question 8: Coin Change
docs.text:
Given a list of coin denominations and a target sum k, return the number of possible ways to make change for that sum.

Technique: Dynamic programming; either tabulation or memoization works but memoization is preferable because not all sub-results are necessary to compute the final result

Approach: For a full write-up and sample code see CoinChange.

Initialize a DP map of maps. The key i in the outer map represents the first i coins used to make the sum j, the key in the inner map. Use a recursive helper function that accepts a number of coins, n, and a sum k in addition to the coin values and DP map. Each time the recursive function is called, do the following:

  1. If the sum k is 0 return 1.
  2. If the number of coins n is 0 return 0.
  3. If the number of coins and sum is already in the DP map, return it.
  4. Otherwise, make two recursive calls: n coins and sum-coins[n-1] (the value of the nth coin); and n-1 coins and sum. Set the value in the DP map to the sum of the two recursive calls and return it.

Big O: O(n*k) time, O(n*k) space

docs.title: Question 9: Adopt a Pet
docs.text:
An animal shelter that houses cats and dogs wants to ensure no pet has to wait too long for a forever home. Therefore, anyone who comes to adopt a pet can pick the species (cat or dog) but not the specific animal; they are assigned the animal of that species that has been in the shelter longest. If there are no animals available of the desired species, they must take the other species. You are given a list of pets in the shelter with their names, species, and time in the shelter at the start of a week. You receive a sequence of incoming people (to adopt pets) and animals (new additions to the shelter) one at a time. Print the names and species of the pets as they are adopted out.

Technique: Maintain two queues

Approach:

Create a queue for each cats and dogs. Sort the initial input by time in descending order and iterate through it, inserting into the appropriate queue based on pet species. Thereafter, when a new pet is received add it the appropriate queue. Remove and print the front of the appropriate queue if a person arrives; be sure to remove from the non-empty queue if the requested queue is empty.

Big O: O(1) time for each pet/person arrival, O(n) overall, O(n) space

  • Attend mentor onboarding (only before workshop 1)

docs.title: 3 Weeks Before Workshop
docs.text:
Regional PgM Lead:

  • Confirm agenda and share with Mentor/Volunteer Lead what volunteers are needed
  • Confirm speakers
  • Host dry runs as needed
  • Update deck

Mentor/Volunteer Lead:

  • Send reminders to fellows to do their technical practice assignments
  • Send mentor reminders to grade technical practice assignments as soon as it’s submitted

docs.title: 2 Weeks Before Workshop
docs.text:
Regional PgM Lead:

  • Finalize agenda and speakers
  • Host dry runs as needed
  • Update deck

Technical Lead:

  • Practice technical session presentation

docs.title: 1 Week Before Workshop
docs.text:
Mentor/Volunteer Lead:

  • Schedule all mock interviews- make sure all calendar invites are PUBLIC and do NOT require authentication to join Zoom
    • Include in all cal invites:
      • Zoom
      • CodeSignal
      • Fellow Name
      • Interviewer Name
      • Resume
      • Zoom Troubleshooting Doc
      • Name of POC in case there are issues
      • Mock Interview Questions Bank

Technical Lead:

  • Review technical session
  • Review upcoming technical practice assignments assignment & solution guide

docs.title: 3 Days Before Workshop
docs.text:
Regional Lead:

  • Send reminder email to fellows with agenda and deck

docs.title: 1 Day Before Workshop
docs.text:
Regional Lead:

  • Check-in with all speakers
  • Close editing to workshop deck

Mentor/Volunteer Lead:

  • Send reminder email to mock interviewers

docs.title: Day of Workshop
docs.text:
Regional PgM Lead:

  • Take lots of photos!
    • Photos of all the students
    • Photos of the Uber presenters
  • Send reminders to all speakers 30 minutes before session
  • Manage zoom breakout sessions
  • Have fellows submit feedback in closing session of workshop

Alumni Lead/MC:

  • Be ready to share screen
  • Be ready with music to play during all breaks

Mentor/Volunteer Lead:

  • Be available to help troubleshoot if anything happens with mock interviews

Technical Lead:

  • Host one hour technical session

docs.title: 2 Days After Workshop
docs.text:
Regional PgM Lead:

  • Send thank you + recap email to students for participating
    • Include technical practice assignments assignment
    • Include master deck + agenda + any other shared resources
    • Include feedback survey
  • Update budget tracker for any spend associated with workshop

Mentor/Volunteer Lead:

  • Send followup emails to volunteers if they haven’t submitted their mock interview feedback yet

docs.title: 2 Weeks After Workshop
docs.text:
Mentor/Volunteer Lead:

  • Make sure all mock interview feedback is submitted by this time
  • Track technical practice assignments submission from fellows
  • Remind mentors to grade technical practice assignments

Technical Lead:

  • Host 1-hour optional technical office hours session to answer questions about the technical practice assignments

docs.title: End of Cohort
docs.text:
Regional PgM:

  • Send recognition emails for volunteers
  • Stay connected with TA Lead for conversion metrics
  • Send cohort metrics to volunteers and key stakeholders
  • Send congratulations email to cohort

Mentor/Volunteer Lead:

  • Send Email thank you’s for mentors and include direct managers
  • Send feedback surveys to mentors
  • Review mentor feedback

TA Lead:

  • Source volunteers for conversion interviews
  • Schedule conversion interviews
  • Track conversions
  • Share conversions with Regional PgM
  • Continually update alumni tracker at the beginning of each new internship / hiring cycle

docs.title: Welcome Deck
docs.text:
The Welcome Deck is included in the acceptance email to fellows as a way to confirm their place in the cohort. It includes an introduction slide template that each fellow completes with their name, pronouns, location, a fun fact and a photo, so the cohort can get to know each other.

Replace the [YEAR], [REGION] and [COMPANY] placeholders with your program's details, and ask each fellow to make a copy of the intro slide.

Download PDF Download PowerPoint (editable)

docs.title: Where it is used
docs.text:
• Program Execution Checklist: include the deck in the welcome email to confirm fellows' places in the cohort.
  • Communications Check-List: cohort acceptance emails, sent with the invite.

docs.title: Roles & Responsibilities
docs.text: Successful execution of a Career Prep program depends on a well-defined team structure. This section outlines every role — both on the Core Program Team and in the broader volunteer pool.

docs.title: Core Program Team
docs.text:
While each role is vital to program execution, they may not require full-time staff. Percentage time is calculated based on a 35-hour week or 8-month cohort.

Role Time Commitment Key Focus Regional Program Lead ~700 hrs (~50% over 8 months) Program logistics, stakeholders, budget Recruiting Team ~436 hrs (~30% over 8 months) Marketing, interviews, offers Workshop MC ~40 hrs (~1% over 8 months) Workshop facilitation Technical Lead ~48 hrs (~3% over 8 months) Technical curriculum, interviews Mentor & Volunteer Lead ~116 hrs (~8% over 8 months) Mentor sourcing, coordination

docs.title: Core Program Team
docs.text: While each role is vital to program execution, they may not require full-time staff. Detailed role descriptions and time commitments are available in the linked resources. Percentage time is calculated based on a 35-hour week or 8-month cohort.

docs.title: Regional Program Lead
docs.text:
Time commitment: ~700 hours (~50% time) over 8-month cohort

The Regional Program Lead is the central coordinator of the entire program.

Responsibilities:

  • Manages program logistics, timeline, stakeholders, and budget
  • Liaises between team and stakeholders
  • Oversees Core Team execution
  • Manages program timeline and milestones
  • Authors/oversees program communications
  • Confirms and creates workshop topics/agendas
  • Identifies workshop speakers
  • Reviews/implements workshop feedback

docs.title: Recruiting Team
docs.text:
Time commitment: ~436 hours (~30% time) over 8-month cohort

Responsibilities:

  • Confirms/finalizes regional internship headcount with the Recruiting Team and organizations
  • Creates marketing materials and leads application marketing/tracking
  • Secures technical/behavioral interviewers for all interviews
  • Schedules/reschedules all interviews
  • Sources applicants via university partnerships and target schools
  • Point of contact for recruiting questions on program Slack channels
  • Follows up with fellows during interviews and extends offers
  • Tracks competitor offers for metrics and industry insights
  • Tracks company offers post-cohort and updates cohort graduate (alumni) tracker

docs.title: Workshop MC
docs.text:
Time commitment: ~40 hours (~1% time) during 8-month cohort

The Workshop MC is the main company representative at each workshop. This role can be combined with the Regional Program Lead if additional headcount is not available. Program alumni make ideal MCs.

Responsibilities:

  • Main company representative at each workshop
  • Manages speaker slides
  • Creates workshop playlists
  • Keeps sessions on time and fellows engaged
  • Triages workshop questions

docs.title: Technical Lead
docs.text:
Time commitment: ~48 hours (~3% time) during 8-month cohort

Responsibilities:

  • Manages technical portion of cohort acceptance interview process:
    • Questions bank
    • Volunteer interview training
    • Score cards/evaluation
    • Reviews scores, makes recommendations/decisions
  • Manages mock interview question bank and score cards
  • Manages internship interview question bank and score cards
  • Authors/hosts technical training for volunteers
  • Authors/hosts 75-min technical sessions for fellows during each workshop
  • Hosts 60-min office hours between workshops
  • Answers technical questions across all channels
  • Creates/maintains code sharing platform for assignments and access

docs.title: Mentor & Volunteer Lead
docs.text:
Time commitment: ~116 hours (~8% time) over 8-month cohort

Responsibilities:

  • Sources/assigns technical mentors for the cohort
  • Liaises between Core Team, mentors, and fellows
  • Manages mock interview sourcing/scheduling for each workshop
  • Tracks mock interview/assignment submissions and follow-ups
  • Provides mentors with workshop recaps
  • Co-hosts office hours with Technical Lead
  • Point of contact for mentor/volunteer questions on Slack

docs.title: Volunteer Roles
docs.text: Volunteers are essential for program execution, fulfilling various roles. The number of volunteers needed depends on their backgrounds, availability, and capacity.

docs.title: Mentors
docs.text:
Time commitment ~2 hours/week Duration Entire cohort (8 months) Eligibility Technical background required (must know how to code)

Responsibilities:

  • Conducts at least two 30-min meetings with their fellow between workshops
  • Attends mentor onboarding and reviews training materials before cohort launch
  • Grades fellow's technical practice assignments
  • Reviews assignments and mock interview feedback with their fellow
  • Updates mentee/mentor data in the mentor tracker for accountability
  • Submits mid-year and year-end program feedback surveys

docs.title: Session Leads
docs.text:
Time commitment Up to 60 min/session Duration Per workshop Eligibility Technical or non-technical background, depending on the workshop theme

Responsibilities:

  • Participates in a 30-minute prep sync to align workshop expectations
  • Develops/updates slides and contributes them to the main workshop deck
  • Confirms which speakers will handle screen sharing
  • Conducts a dry-run if necessary

docs.title: Mock Interviewers
docs.text:
Time commitment 70 minutes/interview (60 min interview + 10 min for feedback submission) Duration Per workshop Eligibility Technical background required (must know how to code)

Responsibilities:

  • Reviews mock interviewer training materials and question bank
  • Reviews the fellow's resume before the interview
  • Conducts the mock interview using the company's preferred platform
  • Provides live feedback in the last 10 minutes, if time allows
  • Submits feedback immediately post-interview

docs.title: Technical Interviewers
docs.text:
Conduct interviews to assess candidate suitability for both cohort admission and potential internship placement.

Time commitment 70 minutes/interview (60 min interview + 10 min for feedback form submission) Duration Cohort entrance interviews and/or internship interviews Eligibility Technical background required (must know how to code); must have completed required company interview trainings

Responsibilities:

  • Reviews interviewer training documents and questions bank
  • Attends the program-specific interviewer training
  • Reviews the fellow's resume before the interview
  • Submits feedback immediately post-interview

docs.title: Behavioral Interviewers
docs.text:
Time commitment 35 minutes/interview (30 min interview + 5 min for feedback form submission) Duration Cohort entrance interviews and/or internship interviews Eligibility No specific background requirements; must have completed required company interview trainings

Responsibilities:

  • Reviews interviewer training documents and questions bank
  • Attends the program-specific interviewer training
  • Reviews the fellow's resume before the interview
  • Submits feedback immediately post-interview

docs.title: Cohort Application Reviewers
docs.text:
Time commitment ~4 minutes/application (total time determined by application-to-volunteer ratio) Duration Application review period Eligibility Technical background recommended

Responsibilities:

  • Attends application reviewer training
  • Adds applicant summaries and reviewer accept/reject recommendations to the applicant tracker
